articles.title: Matt Pocock's Agent Skills: The Markdown Files Everyone's Installing (and Whether They Still Matter)
articles.description: Quick confession: I rolled my eyes when "a folder of Markdown files" started topping GitHub trending....
articles.body_html:
Quick confession: I rolled my eyes when "a folder of Markdown files" started topping GitHub trending. Then I tried it, and I stopped rolling my eyes.

The folder is mattpocock/skills. Let's talk about who's behind it, why it blew up, what's inside, and whether it's still worth your time now that models keep getting smarter.

Wait, who is Matt Pocock?

Not an AI lab researcher, which is part of the charm. His path is a bit unusual:

  • Voice coach first. He came from performing arts and public speaking coaching, then taught himself to code.
  • XState and Stately. He was on the XState core team and a developer advocate at Stately, where he helped bring TypeScript into XState.
  • Vercel. He worked there as a developer advocate. By his own account he took the job as a safety net in case his course didn't work out.
  • Total TypeScript. It did work out. The course passed $2.5M in sales and he left Vercel to teach full time.
  • AI Hero. Launched in July 2025 as a course for web developers retraining as AI engineers, and it became his most successful launch so far.

He's also loud on X (roughly 250k followers), which explains some of the repo's reach.

So the skills come from a teacher who's spent years explaining hard things simply. You can feel that in the files.

The repo, by the numbers

Star counts depend on who you ask and when, so treat these as a rough timeline:

When (2026) What happened
Spring Hit #1 trending within a day and crossed ~22k stars on day one; ~45k by Apr 29, ~58k by May 4
Mid-May Topped GitHub's weekly trending with +1,618 stars
Late July Led the weekly trending list again with +10,651 stars
Early Sept #2 on daily trending, +2,206 stars in 24 hours, ~254k total
Latest trackers ~300k stars, ~27k forks

A few fun facts: it's MIT licensed, GitHub reports it as "Shell 100%" because there's no actual app code, and it has a tiny contributor list. It's basically a personal .claude directory published to the world.

skills.sh and the install counts

Stars are vanity. Installs are closer to usage. skills.sh is Vercel's directory and leaderboard for agent skills (npx skills add owner/repo, works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Copilot and friends). Pocock's skills dominate it. On the all-time board:

Skill All-time rank Installs
grill-me #3 1.6M
grill-with-docs #10 1.3M
grilling #16 1.1M
prototype #18 1.1M
triage #19 1.1M
domain-modeling #25 ~988K
code-review #58 ~900K
implement #61 ~873K

The repo also gets name-dropped in the usual awesome lists, like awesome-claude-code. And one dev who tried the heavier "Superpowers" skill pack wrote that they prefer the leaner grill-me and grill-with-docs, whose entry files are only about seven lines each.

(Install counts include some older skill names, since Pocock reorganizes things often.)

What's actually in it

About 27 skills, split into two kinds:

  • User-invoked: you type them (/grill-me). They orchestrate.
  • Model-invoked: the agent can reach for them when a task fits (tdd, code-review).

The README's rule: a user-invoked skill can call model-invoked ones, never another user-invoked one. Simple and predictable.

The README organizes the skills around four recurring ways agents let you down:

Agent problem Skills that fix it
Builds the wrong thing /grill-me, /grill-with-docs
Way too wordy /grill-with-docs (shared glossary)
Code doesn't work /tdd, /diagnosing-bugs
Codebase becomes spaghetti /to-spec, /improve-codebase-architecture

The skills that save you the most time (with examples)

/grill-me: stop the guessing

Give an agent a fuzzy request and it'll confidently build something. This skill flips it so the agent interviews you first, branch by branch, until the plan is solid.

/grill-me I want to add caching to our /products API

Expect questions like: how stale can data be? What invalidates an entry? Per-user or shared? What happens under a stampede? Ten minutes of questions beats one rejected implementation.

Use /grill-me for general plans and /grill-with-docs when you're inside a codebase.

CONTEXT.md: say one word instead of twenty

The README's point is that agents get dropped into a project and invent their own vocabulary, then burn tokens explaining things the long way. /grill-with-docs fixes that by building a glossary (CONTEXT.md) and decision records (docs/adr/) as you talk.

Say your team calls it a "booking", but the code has "reservation", "order" and "slot". The agent spots the clash, you pick "booking", and it's written down. Now names are consistent, the agent searches with the right term, and replies get shorter. That's a direct token saving.

/tdd and /diagnosing-bugs: give the agent a feedback loop

An agent with no failing test is flying blind. /tdd runs red-green-refactor, one thin vertical slice at a time:

/tdd Add a 10% discount for orders over $100

One failing test, minimum code to pass, tidy, next behavior. /diagnosing-bugs does the same for nasty bugs: reproduce, minimize, hypothesize, instrument, fix, add a regression test. No more "random edits and vibes".

Specs, tickets and parallel agents

  • /to-spec turns the conversation into a spec on your tracker.
  • /to-tickets splits it into small tickets with dependencies.
  • /implement builds it (using /tdd, and /code-review before commit).
  • /implement-spec runs parallel subagents over a task graph.
  • /wayfinder handles projects too big for one session.

Keeping context clean

  • /handoff condenses a long session into a doc a fresh agent can pick up.
  • /wait-what re-explains a confusing message in plain English.
  • /retro suggests improvements to your agent setup after a session.
  • /improve-codebase-architecture finds modules worth deepening and shows them in an HTML report. It surveys, it doesn't fix legacy messes for you.

Okay, but is it still relevant with newer models?

Fair question. Models improve every few months, and a lot of prompt tricks die fast. Here's my honest read:

Why it's holding up:

  • These skills are mostly process, not model workarounds. Clarifying requirements, shared vocabulary, tests and small slices help human teams too, and that doesn't expire when a model upgrades.
  • Pocock keeps updating the repo and uses it with current models. As of mid-2026 he said he was still mostly on Opus 4.8 and cautious about fully switching to the newest one, and a recent release added a wait-what skill aimed at Opus being wordy.
  • His AI Engineer Europe 2026 talk makes the argument directly: AI-assisted development leans on shared design concepts, precise domain language, fast feedback loops and humans owning the design.
  • The skills are tiny. A seven-line skill costs almost nothing in context, so there's little downside to keeping it.

Where I'd stay skeptical (this part is my opinion):

  • Some skills compensate for specific model habits (rambling, not asking questions). As models get better at that on their own, those skills may matter less.
  • Nobody has published rigorous benchmarks showing before/after gains. The evidence is installs, stars and user testimonials, which show popularity rather than proven efficiency.
  • A skill that fires too often can waste context. Install the ones you'll actually use, not all 27.

My take: treat it as a toolbox, not a religion. Start with /grill-me, add /tdd, and see what sticks.

Getting started in 60 seconds 

npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills

Pick your skills (include setup-matt-pocock-skills), then run /setup-matt-pocock-skills once per repo. Claude Code users can also use the plugin route:

claude plugin marketplace add mattpocock/skills
claude plugin install mattpocock-skills@mattpocock

Lost? Type /ask-matt and it'll point you to the right skill.

A simple loop: /grill-with-docs → /to-spec → /to-tickets → /implement → /handoff when the session gets long → /retro at the end.

Wrap-up

The magic isn't any single prompt. It's the habit: spend your human attention early (clarify the plan, agree on words), then give the agent tight feedback (tests, small slices, reviews). Do that and you get fewer retries, shorter answers and code you can reason about.

Try one skill this week. What's the one you'd install first?

articles.title: Next.js use cache Reused the Same Cache Entry for Different Files Before 16.4.5
articles.description: The Next.js docs tell you that the serializable arguments you pass to a use cache function become...
articles.body_html:
The Next.js docs tell you that the serializable arguments you pass to a use cache function become part of its cache key. They even list which types are supported. What they don't show is how binary values end up in that key, or what quietly falls out of it. That gap matters, because a cache key is a promise. Two calls with the same key get the same answer, and if the key is missing something, one caller can end up with another caller's result.

So I stopped guessing and tested it. I ran 54 pairs of different inputs through use cache on Next.js 16.4.4, 16.4.5 and 16.4.6, then opened the code that builds the key to find out why the results looked the way they did. Some of it surprised me. Two File objects with the same bytes but different names got the same cache entry. So did a byte array with an odd number of bytes and the same array with one extra zero byte on the end. It lines up with a security advisory Next.js published with the 16.4.5 fix, GHSA-rhh4-g77r-r9qj, and I'll get to that below.

I ran the tests with next start, the default in-memory cache handler and cacheComponents set to true, calling cached functions from route handlers and one Server Action page. The demo reproduces with one command (npm run demo) and the rest of the lab takes a few more. The code is in nextjs-use-cache-key-lab.

The short version

If you only have a minute, this is what I found.

  • Most inputs behave the way you'd hope. On 16.4.6, 46 of my 54 pairs of different inputs got their own cache entry.
  • Until 16.4.5, two different binary values could share one cache entry. The key ignored a File's name and type. It treated a Blob and a File with the same bytes as one value. It also treated a byte array with an odd number of bytes as identical to that array plus one trailing zero byte. 16.4.5 fixed all of that.
  • File.lastModified still isn't part of the key, and the source says that's on purpose. For a form upload it's only the time your server parsed the request.
  • Values the cache can't read (class instances, functions, RegExp, Symbols) share one entry when your function ignores them, and throw when a closure captures them.
  • A Uint8Array or Blob argument over about 250,000 bytes throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded, and the exact threshold depends on your machine. I found the line of code behind it, and it reproduces in plain Node.

What goes into a Next.js use cache key

The docs list the parts of a use cache key. There's the build ID (or your deploymentId if you've set one, which overrides it), a function ID, the serializable arguments you pass, and in development an HMR hash. Variables your function captures from an outer scope are bound as arguments too, so they count as well. If you're new to all of this, my Next.js 16 Cache Components migration guide covers the basics, and the official use cache docs are the reference.

The build ID and the function ID aren't interesting. They're the same for every call of the same function in the same build. The arguments are where the surprises live, so that's what I tested.

How I tested the use cache key

The idea is simple. For each case I build two values that differ in exactly one way. Then I call the same cached function with value A, with A again (a control, to prove the call really is cached), and finally with value B. The function returns a fresh marker every time it actually runs. In my harness that's a random token, and in the short examples below it's a timestamp. If B gets A's marker back, B reused A's cache entry.

Sharing an entry isn't always a problem, though. I also compute what B should have seen without any cache. That separates a harmless alias from a wrong answer.

Status Meaning
SEPARATE B got its own entry
SHARED B reused A's entry, and the output is what B would have produced anyway
SHARED-WRONG B reused A's entry and received output computed for a different input

I ran this on three versions on my machine, 16.4.4, 16.4.5 and 16.4.6. Across those three the results change at exactly one boundary, between 16.4.4 and 16.4.5. If turning on cacheComponents breaks your own build before you can even test this, I wrote up the errors I hit in Every Way I Could Break Next.js Cache Components.

The repo also holds reference results for 12 versions (16.0.0 to 16.4.6, plus Node 20 and 24 for two of them). They come from a second machine, not mine. In those, the key results are identical on every version up to 16.4.4, and identical on 16.4.5 and 16.4.6. I didn't run the other versions myself, so I treat that as supporting data and not as part of my own test.

The results

Read the bold rows first.

What differs between A and B 16.4.4 16.4.5 and 16.4.6
Strings, numbers, booleans, BigInt, null vs undefined, 0 vs -0, '1' vs 1, undefined vs the string '$undefined' SEPARATE SEPARATE
Object values, nested values, [1,2] vs [2,1], an array vs an object with numeric keys, {} vs [] SEPARATE SEPARATE
Object key order swapped ({a, b} vs {b, a}) SEPARATE SEPARATE
Map, Set and FormData insertion order swapped SEPARATE SEPARATE
Date, Map and Set values, FormData, URL, URLSearchParams SEPARATE SEPARATE
Typed arrays with different bytes, only the last byte of 200,000, Uint8 vs Int8, Uint8 vs ArrayBuffer, Uint8 vs Buffer SEPARATE SEPARATE
Blob or File with different bytes, only the last byte of 200,000 SEPARATE SEPARATE
Array hole [1,,3] vs [1, undefined, 3] SHARED (harmless) SHARED (harmless)
Same 4 bytes as a standalone array vs a view into a bigger buffer SHARED (harmless) SHARED (harmless)
File name differs (same bytes) SHARED-WRONG SEPARATE
Blob or File type differs (same bytes) SHARED-WRONG SEPARATE
Blob vs File (same bytes) SHARED-WRONG SEPARATE
Odd-length binary value vs the same value plus one trailing 0 byte (Uint8Array, Blob, File) SHARED-WRONG SEPARATE
File.lastModified differs SHARED-WRONG SHARED-WRONG
Class instance, function, RegExp or Symbol that the function ignores SHARED SHARED

The totals are 38 SEPARATE, 7 SHARED and 9 SHARED-WRONG on 16.4.4, and 46 SEPARATE, 7 SHARED and 1 SHARED-WRONG on 16.4.6. The full 54-row table is in the repo.

Bob gets Alice's file

The easiest way to see the problem is a tiny cached function that takes a File.

// lib/inspect.js
"use cache";

export async function inspectUpload(file) {
  return {
    name: file.name,
    type: file.type,
    size: file.size,
    filledAt: Date.now(),
  };
}

I call it with two Files that hold the same 32 bytes but have different names. This is real output from my run on 16.4.4.

inspectUpload(File "alice.pdf") -> { "name": "alice.pdf", ... "filledAt": 1794584074839 }
inspectUpload(File "bob.pdf")   -> { "name": "alice.pdf", ... "filledAt": 1794584074839 }

Look at the second line. Bob's call got Alice's result. The filledAt value is identical, so the function body never even ran. On 16.4.5, Bob gets bob.pdf, as you would expect.

The byte-level case is stranger. Take this function.

export async function describeBytes(bytes) {
  return {
    length: bytes.length,
    last: bytes[bytes.length - 1],
    filledAt: Date.now(),
  };
}

On 16.4.4, describeBytes(Uint8Array.from([61, 62, 63])) returns length: 3, which is correct. Then I call describeBytes(Uint8Array.from([61, 62, 63, 0])), a different array with four bytes. It also returns length: 3. On 16.4.5 it returns length: 4.

One caveat before I go on. The docs list TypedArrays and ArrayBuffers as supported arguments, but they don't mention Blob or File. So what I report for those two is observed behaviour in the versions I tested, not a documented guarantee.

One extra zero byte, and the cache couldn't tell the difference.

Does the use cache File bug happen through a real form upload?

Everything above calls the cached function from a route handler. In a real app a File usually arrives through a Server Action, so I tested that path too. It's a plain <form action={upload}>, where the action takes formData.get('file') and passes it to the same cached inspectUpload. I posted the form the way a browser without JavaScript would. I wrote about other Server Action problems in Next.js 16 Server Actions and the bugs that only show up in production.

The result was the same. On 16.4.4 the bob.pdf upload returned alice.pdf's result, and a 4-byte file returned the result for the 3-byte file before it. On 16.4.5 each upload got its own result. Inside the action the value was a real File. You can run it with npm run action.

Why this happens

The code that builds the key lives in Next's server bundle, not in your code. Your arguments go through React's reply encoder first. When one of them holds binary data, the result is a FormData, and a function called encodeFormData turns that into the string used in the key. You can read it in node_modules/next/dist/server/use-cache/use-cache-wrapper.js in all three versions I tested, and my diagnose script also prints the minified copy from the build output. What follows is a simplified, renamed copy of the binary branch of encodeFormData as it was in 16.4.4, the last version before the fix. It's not a drop-in copy of Next's key builder. The diagnose output in the repo's reference results shows the same fields missing from the key in every build from 16.0.0 to 16.4.4, but I didn't run those versions myself.

async function encodeFormData(formData) {
  let key = "";
  for (const [field, value] of formData) {
    let text;
    key += field.length.toString(16) + ":" + field;
    if (typeof value === "string") {
      text = value;
    } else {
      const buf = await value.arrayBuffer();
      text =
        buf.byteLength % 2 === 0
          ? String.fromCodePoint(...new Uint16Array(buf))
          : String.fromCodePoint(
              ...new Uint16Array(buf, 0, (buf.byteLength - 1) / 2),
            ) +
            String.fromCodePoint(new Uint8Array(buf, buf.byteLength - 1, 1)[0]);
    }
    key += text.length.toString(16) + ":" + text;
  }
  return key;
}

Here's what that means. The bytes become a string, two bytes at a time, and that's all that goes into the key for that argument. There's no name, no type, and no record of whether it was a Blob or a File. On top of that, an odd number of bytes ends with a lone byte, which gets read as one code unit. On a little-endian CPU (x86 and, in practice, ARM) that's the same code unit you get from reading [x, 0] as a 16-bit number. So [61, 62, 63] and [61, 62, 63, 0] produce the same string with the same length. Replaying the logic shows that even-length arrays don't collide this way. Adding a zero byte to an even-length array makes it odd-length, and an odd-length array gets its lone byte appended as an extra code unit, so the two strings differ. My lab tests the 3-byte and 4-byte case, so the even-length part comes from reading the code and not from a run.

From 16.4.5 the binary branch also writes the name, the type and the byte length before the text.

key +=
  "B" +
  value.name.length.toString(16) +
  ":" +
  value.name +
  value.type.length.toString(16) +
  ":" +
  value.type +
  buf.byteLength.toString(16) +
  ":" +
  text;

Reading minified code is one thing, but I also wanted to see the real keys, so I wrote a small cache handler that wraps Next's default one and logs every key it receives. This is output from my run. The hex ids differ per build, so compare the two lines inside one version.

16.4.4  alice.pdf  1:110:܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇1:050:["c084f7f0…",["$B1"],["VTD4as…"]]   miss
16.4.4  bob.pdf    1:110:܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇1:050:["c084f7f0…",["$B1"],["VTD4as…"]]   HIT, same string

16.4.5  alice.pdf  1:1B9:alice.pdf0:20:܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇1:050:["c02d82da…",["$B1"],["noVPW1…"]]
16.4.5  bob.pdf    1:1B7:bob.pdf0:20:܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇܇1:050:["c02d82da…",["$B1"],["noVPW1…"]]

The odd character is U+0707. My 32 bytes, each with the value 7, are read two at a time as sixteen 16-bit code units. On 16.4.4 the two keys are the same string, so the second call is a hit. On 16.4.5 the file name is in the key. The same experiment for [61,62,63] and [61,62,63,0] shows 0:3: against 0:4: on 16.4.5, which is the byte length that 16.4.4 left out. You can run it yourself with npm run keys.

That one change explains every row that flipped. It also explains why lastModified didn't flip, because it isn't in that line. You can print this function from your own build with npm run diagnose, so you don't have to take my word for it.

Is this the use cache cross-user cache disclosure advisory?

It matches. Next.js's November 3 security release lists Cross-user cache disclosure and poisoning through binary use cache arguments. The GitHub advisory for it (GHSA-rhh4-g77r-r9qj, CVE-2026-119349) is rated Moderate there, while the release post says Medium. It lists 16.0.0 through 16.4.4 as affected and 16.4.5 as the fix. It says that applications passing binary arguments "(such as Uint8Array or Blob values)" to use cache functions "can produce identical cache keys for distinct arguments".

My results line up with that. On 16.4.4 I got identical key strings for different File and Uint8Array values, and shared results for Blob values too (I didn't print the Blob keys). The key function changed in 16.4.5. I only ran 16.4.4, 16.4.5 and 16.4.6 myself, so the rest of the affected range is the advisory's word and not my measurement. I didn't try to exploit anything. What my lab shows is incorrect cache reuse, and how exposed you are depends on your app and your cache handler.

Does this affect your app?

The advisory is careful about this, and you should be too. It says the risk applies when an application uses binary arguments "to distinguish users or accounts", the remaining cache-identity inputs match, and the entries are shared across callers. It adds that this "does not permit arbitrary access to unrelated cache entries."

In my tests the practical version is that a collision needs a function whose output depends on something the key ignored. This specific collision doesn't apply to functions that take only strings and numbers. The concern is when distinct binary values change what the function returns but the key treats them as the same. If you pass a File and return something derived from its name or type, or you identify a user with a byte array, upgrade to 16.4.5 or later. The docs also say that with the default in-memory handler, entries typically don't persist across serverless requests, and hosts can replace the cache handler. So your exposure depends on where you host.

The same security release has other use cache advisories, for nested functions and for unstable_cache. They are different bugs and this article doesn't cover them.

There's one more thing if you run old versions. A separate advisory (GHSA-673q-mjm6-r5xr, Critical, no CVE) describes unauthenticated remote code execution in App Router apps with Cache Components that have a use cache function returning multiple typed arrays. It affects 16.0.0 through 16.4.0, it's fixed in 16.4.1, and the advisory says there's no known workaround. The three versions I tested aren't in that range and my lab doesn't trigger it. It's still a good reason not to run old versions anywhere reachable from the internet.

Is File.lastModified part of the use cache key?

No, and that looks deliberate. Two Files with the same bytes, name and type but different lastModified share one entry on 16.4.6. The second caller receives the first caller's value.

The readable source that ships with 16.4.5 and 16.4.6 (next/dist/server/use-cache/use-cache-wrapper.js) has a comment next to the key builder. It says the name and type are part of the key because the cached function observes them. It also says "lastModified is excluded", and that it "defaults to the construction time and does not survive multipart submission."

I checked the second half of that comment in the lab's Server Action test on 16.4.6. I uploaded a file with lastModified set to 1000, and the action saw the server's current time instead. A File you build without that option also gets the current time as its lastModified, and the MDN page for the File constructor documents the option. So for form uploads, lastModified is when your server parsed the request. Don't read it inside a cached function and expect the date from the user's file.

What about values the cache can't read?

The docs say you can pass non-serializable values "as long as you don't introspect them". I wanted to know what that means in practice, so I tested two situations. One is passing the value as an argument. The other is capturing it in a closure inside the cached function.

Value Passed as an argument (the function never reads the opaque ones) Captured by a closure inside the cached function
Class instance one shared entry throws
Function one shared entry throws
RegExp one shared entry throws
Symbol('a') one shared entry throws
Symbol.for('a') one shared entry one shared entry if only mentioned, throws if read
Date, Map, Set, plain object separate entries separate entries

One shared entry means that, for example, Symbol.for('a') and Symbol.for('b') get the same cached result. That's by design, since the function isn't supposed to read them. It's still worth knowing, because it means these values never affect the key. The errors are the generic Flight ones. One example is "Only plain objects, and a few built-ins, can be passed to Client Components from Server Components. Classes or null prototypes are not supported." Reading a captured Symbol.for logs "Cannot access constructor on the server" on the server.

One more oddity. The docs list URL instances as unsupported, but a URL worked as an argument in my tests. It arrived inside the function as a string, and different URLs got separate entries. I wouldn't rely on that.

Cache misses you create without noticing

Now the opposite problem. These all got separate entries, which is correct, but each one is a potential extra miss.

  • An object with its keys in a different order is a different entry.
  • Map, Set and FormData insertion order matters.
  • 0 and -0 are different, and so are null and undefined.
  • An object with a shared reference is different from two equal copies.

Nothing here is a bug. If you build argument objects in different places, pass primitives like an id or a string instead and let the function look the rest up.

What is the maximum argument size for use cache?

A binary argument over a certain size throws.

RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded

On my machine the largest Uint8Array that works in a fresh process is 250,871 bytes. At 250,872 it throws, though the threshold moves a little as the process warms up, as you will see below. On a second machine the same test stopped at about 247,000, so the exact number depends on your machine and Node version, and I'd treat anything near 250,000 as the edge.

Blob fails at about the same size (I didn't measure File separately). Typed arrays fail at about the same number of bytes whatever their element type, which is 125,435 elements for Uint16Array and 31,358 for Float64Array. Across the three versions I ran, the Uint8Array limit never changed, but the others moved by a few dozen bytes. Uint16Array was 125,447 on 16.4.4 and 16.4.5 and 125,435 on 16.4.6, and Blob measured 250,895 in one run and 250,871 in another. So read these numbers as "about", not exact.

The cause looks like the String.fromCodePoint(...new Uint16Array(buf)) line from earlier. As the MDN page for String.fromCodePoint shows, it takes its input as separate arguments, so the spread passes one function argument per two bytes, and each argument takes a slot on the call stack. Two things back this up.

  • It reproduces without Next.js. String.fromCodePoint(...new Uint16Array(n)) in plain Node fails above about 125,235 elements.
  • It moves with warm-up. On a fresh process 250,872 bytes failed. After 300 other requests the same size passed, and the warmed-up maximum was 250,899.

The lab also has a --stack-size experiment. I haven't run it on my own machine, so I'm not making a claim about it. In the reference run from the second machine the limit roughly halved at --stack-size=500 and roughly doubled at 2000, which fits the stack explanation, but that isn't my own measurement.

So there's no exact number to memorise. Treat about 240 KB as the ceiling on a default stack, and stay far below it. And please don't raise --stack-size in production to dodge this. Pass less.

Buffers and strings have a separate limit. A Node Buffer fails at exactly 1,000,000 bytes and a string at about 999,930 characters, with a different error. The message is "Maximum array nesting exceeded. Large nested arrays can be dangerous. Try adding intermediate objects." It comes from React's Flight decoder, which has a default arraySizeLimit of 1e6. I didn't trace why Buffers and strings count against it. In the reference results from the second machine, this limit is absent on 16.0.0 and 16.1.0 and present from 16.1.7. I haven't run those versions myself.

So what would I actually do?

  1. Upgrade to 16.4.5 or later if you pass binary values to use cache at all.
  2. Pass ids, not files. Store the upload, pass its id (a string), and read the bytes inside the cached function. The id must change when the content changes, and a content hash or a version number works. If you reuse one id for edited content, the cache will happily return the old result. A sketch follows. 
   export async function analyze(fileId) {
     "use cache";
     const bytes = await storage.read(fileId); // read inside the cache
     return expensiveAnalysis(bytes);
   }
  1. Never use a binary value as a user or account identifier in a cached function's arguments.
  2. Keep arguments small. My rule of thumb is to stay under about 100 KB, which leaves a wide margin below the limit.
  3. Pass only the metadata your function reads, and not File.lastModified from a form upload. On 16.4.4, passing name, type and size as separate arguments stopped the name, type and trailing-byte collisions I found (npm run workaround). The lastModified case stayed shared until I passed it too. On 16.4.5 and later those three are already in the key. lastModified isn't, and for a file that came through a multipart form it's the time your server parsed the request, so passing it as an argument can create unnecessary cache misses on every upload. If you need a modified date, send it as a separate form field.
  4. Pass primitives rather than objects you build in different places.

What I didn't test

I'd rather tell you where my results stop than let you find out the hard way.

  • A second cache handler (Redis, use cache: remote) or use cache: private.
  • Page and component renders. I called cached functions from route handlers and from one Server Action.
  • next dev, and runtimes other than Node.
  • Even-length byte arrays with a trailing zero. The code says they don't collide, but my lab only runs the 3-byte against 4-byte case.
  • Versions other than 16.4.4, 16.4.5 and 16.4.6. The repo's reference results cover 12 versions, but they come from a second machine and not from me.
  • Next.js 15.x. The release post says 15.5.29 got patches in the same release, but I only tested 16.x, so I make no claim about 15.
  • Other operating systems and Node versions. My own runs used one setup, and the second machine matched on the key results.
  • I read the compiled JavaScript that ships in each version, not Next's TypeScript source.

Run it yourself

The repo has the tests and the reference results, so you can check any of this yourself. It takes a few commands.

git clone https://github.com/shubhrapokhariya/nextjs-use-cache-key-lab.git
cd nextjs-use-cache-key-lab
npm run demo        # the two examples above (the first run installs Next.js, so it takes a while)
npm run quick       # 54 input pairs on 16.4.4, 16.4.5, 16.4.6
npm run summarize
npm run diagnose    # prints the key function from your own build
npm run keys        # prints the real cache keys for the alice/bob and trailing-zero cases
npm run action      # the same bug through a Server Action with a form upload
npm run workaround  # which extra arguments avoid which collisions
npm run limits      # the size experiments

npm run quick tests three versions. npm run full tests all 12 and takes much longer. The limits script includes the optional stack-size experiment, and the README shows how to skip it if it fails on your machine. The lab installs old Next.js versions that have known security advisories, so run it on a throwaway machine and not on a server.

The 54 input pairs are in template/app/lib/cases.js. If you find a case that behaves differently on your machine, I'd really like to know.

Next.js ships often, so I'll update this post if the behaviour changes.

Over to you

  1. Do any of your use cache functions take a File, a Blob or a byte array? Which ones would you check first?
  2. Has use cache surprised you with an argument type, or a key behaviour I didn't test?

Leave a comment if you've seen something similar. If you find an input pair the lab doesn't cover, feel free to open an issue on the repo with the two inputs and your Next.js version. I'd be happy to take a look.

articles.title: Swagger UI is from 2011. It’s Time to Upgrade to Scalar.
articles.description: You've built a modern backend with TypeScript, NestJS, or Fastify. Clean architecture, type-safe...
articles.body_html:
You've built a modern backend with TypeScript, NestJS, or Fastify. Clean architecture, type-safe APIs, and everything working perfectly.

Then someone opens your /docs endpoint.

And there it is. The same old Swagger UI.

Don't get me wrong. Swagger UI is great and has served developers for years. But API documentation can look and feel much better.

That's where Scalar comes in.

What Is Scalar?

Scalar is an open-source API documentation tool that gives your OpenAPI documentation a cleaner, more modern interface.

Think of it as Swagger UI, but with a better developer experience.

Here's what makes it interesting:

  • Modern UI: Clean layout, dark mode, and customizable themes.
  • Built-in API client: Test endpoints directly without switching to Postman.
  • Code snippets: Generate request examples in JavaScript, Python, Go, and more.
  • Authentication: Support for Bearer tokens, API keys, and other OpenAPI security schemes.
  • OpenAPI support: Works with your existing OpenAPI specifications.

And the best part?

You don't need to change your backend or rewrite your API schemas.

Swagger UI vs. Scalar

Here's a quick comparison:

Feature Swagger UI Scalar
UI Design Traditional accordion layout Modern, clean interface
Dark Mode Requires customization Built-in
API Testing Basic Try it out Integrated API client
Code Snippets Configurable request snippets Multiple languages and clients
Authentication Bearer, API keys, OAuth2 Bearer, API keys, OAuth2
Search Endpoint filtering Integrated reference search
Customization CSS and configuration Built-in themes and configuration
OpenAPI 3.1 Supported Supported
Open Source Yes Yes

Both tools do the job, but Scalar focuses more on the overall developer experience, especially when exploring and testing APIs.

How Easy Is It to Integrate?

If you're using Fastify with @fastify/swagger already configured, it's just a few lines.

Install Scalar:

npm install @scalar/fastify-api-reference

Register it in your Fastify application:

await fastify.register(
  import('@scalar/fastify-api-reference'),
  {
    routePrefix: '/docs',
    configuration: {
      theme: 'purple',
    },
  }
);

Now open:

http://localhost:3000/docs

That's it. Your existing OpenAPI specification now has a modern documentation interface.

Scalar also supports NestJS, Express, Next.js, and other frameworks.

Should You Replace Swagger UI?

Not necessarily.

Swagger UI is still actively maintained and supports OpenAPI 3.1, authentication, and interactive requests.

Scalar simply offers a different, more polished experience for exploring and testing APIs.

If you're happy with Swagger UI, there's no reason to rush.

But if you want better-looking, developer-friendly API documentation without much effort, Scalar is definitely worth trying.

Final Thoughts

We spend hours improving our backend architecture, performance, and code quality.

Why not give the same attention to our API documentation?

A great API deserves a great developer experience.

Give Scalar a try on your next project.

What do you use for API documentation — Swagger UI, Scalar, or something else?

articles.body_html:
AI agents and AI coding assistants have changed how we approach software development, making it easier to turn ideas into functional applications.
For software developers, one of the best ways to improve your skills and demonstrate your abilities is by building projects that solve real-world problems and have practical use cases.

In this tutorial, you'll learn how to build a modern invoicing application that allows businesses to set up their profiles, create beautifully customized invoices, and send them directly to their clients' email addresses.

I'll also walk you through setting up Firebase for user authentication, real-time database operations, and file storage, and then share the AI prompts for designing and building the entire application with Claude Code, giving you a practical starting point for developing modern, full-stack web applications with AI agents.

Prerequisites

You don’t need prior experience with React or Next.js to build this application. However, having a basic understanding of React and Next.js will help you follow the code and understand how the different parts of the application work.

We will use the following tools and services to build the project:

  • Firebase: A Backend-as-a-Service (BaaS) platform that provides the services we need for the application, including Firebase Authentication for user authentication, Cloud Firestore for storing and managing application data, and Cloud Storage for uploading and storing files.
  • jsPDF: A JavaScript library for generating PDF documents. We’ll use it to generate PDF versions of invoices.
  • Zernio Email API: An email API for sending invoices directly to clients’ email addresses, with the generated PDF invoices included as attachments.

App Overview

Before we start building, let’s look at how the invoicing application works and what users can do with it.

  • Create an account: Users visit the application homepage and click the call-to-action button to create an account using their business email address or personal email address (for freelancers).
  • Set up a business profile: After registering, users provide their business information, including their business name, logo, address, default currency, and payment details.
  • Create invoices: Once their business profile is set up, users are redirected to the dashboard, where they can add customers and create customized invoices using any of the pre-built invoice templates. Each invoice includes the issuer’s and client’s addresses, invoice subject, line items, payment details, total amount, and any additional notes for the recipient.
  • Send or download invoices: Users can send invoices directly to their clients’ email addresses from the application. Alternatively, they can download the invoices as PDFs, send them manually, or print copies for their clients.
  • Track invoices and payments: The dashboard provides an overview of invoices sent, including total amounts grouped by currency and payment history organised by customer or invoice status. Users can track invoices marked as paid, outstanding, overdue, or draft. When a customer makes a payment, users can manually update the invoice’s payment status.

Below is a video walkthrough of the application, showing its interface and key features:

Setting Up Firebase

Firebase is a Backend-as-a-Service (BaaS) platform that provides the infrastructure and services for building web and mobile applications. It handles essential backend functionality, including database management, user authentication, and file storage, so developers can focus on building their applications without having to manage all the underlying server infrastructure.

For our invoicing application, we'll use three Firebase services:

  • Cloud Firestore: To store and manage application data, including business profiles, customer information, and invoices.
  • Firebase Authentication: To handle user registration and sign-in using email/password and Google authentication.
  • Cloud Storage: To upload and store files, such as business logos and printable invoices.

To integrate Firebase into your Next.js application, follow the steps below.

Step 1: Create a new Firebase project

Visit the Firebase Console and sign in with your Google account. Click Create a new Firebase project to get started.

Enter a name for your project and click Continue. On the next screen, you can choose whether to enable Google Analytics for your project. Analytics is optional, so you can disable it if you don't need it.

If you choose to enable Analytics, select an existing Google Analytics account or create a new one. Once you've configured these settings, click Create project and wait for Firebase to finish setting up your project.

Step 2: Add a web app to your Firebase project

From your Firebase project dashboard, click Add app and select the Web (</>) icon to register a new web application.

Enter a nickname for your application and choose whether you want to set up Firebase Hosting. For this tutorial, we won't be using Firebase Hosting, so you can leave that option unchecked.

Click Register app to complete the registration process. Firebase will then generate a configuration object containing the credentials and project information required to connect your Next.js application to Firebase.

Keep this configuration; we'll need it when integrating Firebase into our application.

Step 3: Set up Firestore, Authentication, and Storage

Now that we've created our Firebase project and registered the web application, let’s enable the required Firebase services.

1. Set up Cloud Firestore

From the Firebase Console sidebar, navigate to Databases & Storage > Firestore and click Create database to create a new database for your invoicing application.

Select the Standard edition, choose a database location closest to your target users, and select Production mode when prompted to configure your initial security rules.

Click Create to finish setting up your database.

Note that Production mode initially denies read and write access from client applications. We'll need to configure the appropriate Firestore Security Rules soon.

2. Set up Cloud Storage

Next, navigate to Databases & Storage > Storage to configure file storage for your application.

Click Get started and follow the instructions to create your default storage bucket.

Important: Cloud Storage for Firebase currently requires your project to be on the Blaze (pay-as-you-go) plan. You'll need to link a Google Cloud Billing account and provide a payment method before you can create your storage bucket. Be aware that usage beyond applicable free allowances may incur charges.

3. Set up Firebase Authentication

Finally, navigate to Authentication from the Firebase Console sidebar and click Get started to configure user authentication.

Under the Sign-in method tab, enable the following authentication providers:

  • Email/Password: Enable email and password authentication. Leave the Email link (passwordless sign-in) option disabled.
  • Google: Enable Google authentication, select your email address as the project's support email, and save your changes.

Congratulations! You've successfully created your Firebase project and configured the essential services for your invoicing application.

Database Design for the Invoice App

In this section, you will learn how to structure the database for our invoicing application to ensure efficient data management and make it easier to create, retrieve, and manage invoices.

Before we proceed, it’s important to understand the three main entities in our application and how they relate to one another:

  1. User: Represents the business or individual issuing the invoices. Each user can manage multiple customers and create multiple invoices for them.
  2. Customer: Represents the recipient of an invoice. A customer can receive multiple invoices from the same business.
  3. Invoice: Represents an invoice issued by a business to a customer. Each invoice belongs to a user and is associated with a specific customer.

In addition to these records, we’ll use Firebase Storage to store files associated with the application, including business logos and generated PDF versions of invoices.

The diagram below shows how we’ll organize the data in Cloud Firestore, with the files stored in Firebase Storage.

Firebase Users Collection

When a user signs up or signs in to the application for the first time, a new document is created in the Firestore users collection using their Firebase Authentication UID as the document ID (users/{uid}). This document stores the user’s account information, business details, payment settings, and application preferences.

The document contains the following fields:

Field

Type

Description

uid

string

Firebase Authentication UID, also used as the document ID.

username

string

User’s display name provided during sign-up.

email

string

User’s sign-in email address.

business

map

Business information (see BUSINESS).

payment

map

Default payment information (see PAYMENT).

zernio

map

Zernio Email API configuration (see ZERNIO).

emailDesign

string

Default invoice email design, e.g. monolith.

invoicePrefix

string

Prefix used when generating invoice numbers, e.g. INV-.

invoiceCounter

number

Number of invoices created. The next invoice number is generated using the counter.

defaultDueDays

number

Default payment term in days, e.g. 14.

setupComplete

boolean

Indicates whether the user has completed the business setup process.

createdAt

timestamp

Timestamp indicating when the user document was created, generated using Firebase server time.

When a user first signs up, the business and payment maps are initially empty, while setupComplete is set to false. These fields are updated when the user completes the business setup process and provides their business and payment information.

The business, payment, and zernio maps hold the user’s business details, payment information, and Zernio Email API configuration, respectively. The emailDesign field stores the default email design used when sending invoices to customers.

Firebase Clients Collection

Since each user can have multiple clients, we’ll create a nested clients subcollection under each user’s document. This allows us to organise client records by business, making it easier to manage and retrieve the clients associated with a particular user.

The collection follows this structure in Firestore:

users/{uid}/clients/{clientId}

Here, {uid} represents the user’s Firebase Authentication UID and {clientId} represents the unique document ID assigned to each client. Each document in the clients subcollection stores information about an individual client.

The table below shows the fields we’ll store for each client:

Field

Type

Description

clientId

string

Unique client document ID.

name

string

Client’s name or company name.

contactName

string

Name of the primary contact person.

email

string

Billing email address, pre-filled when sending an invoice.

phone

string

Client’s phone number.

address

map

Client’s address, including street, city, state, postalCode, and country.

taxId

string

Client’s tax identification number or VAT number, displayed on invoices.

currency

string

Default billing currency for the client.

notes

string

Internal notes about the client, visible only to the business.

invoiceCount

number

Total number of invoices created for the client.

totalBilled

number

Cumulative value of the client’s invoices.

createdAt

timestamp

Timestamp indicating when the client document was created, generated using Firebase server time.

Firebase Invoices Collection

Similar to the clients collection, we’ll create a nested invoices subcollection under each user’s document. This ensures that every invoice created by a business is associated with the user who issued it.

The collection follows this structure in Firestore:

users/{uid}/invoices/{invoiceId}

Here, {uid} represents the business owner’s Firebase Authentication UID, while {invoiceId} represents the unique document ID assigned to each invoice. Each document stores the invoice details, including the associated client, business information, line items, payment details, and invoice status.

The table below shows the fields we’ll store for each invoice:

Field

Type

Description

invoiceId

string

Unique invoice document ID.

number

string

Formatted invoice number, e.g. INV-001.

seq

number

Sequential invoice number: 1, 2, 3, etc.

clientId

string

ID of the client associated with the invoice.

clientOrderNumber

number

Sequential invoice count for the specific client, e.g. #001, #002.

client

map

Snapshot of the client’s details when the invoice is issued.

business

map

Snapshot of the business details when the invoice is issued.

template

string

Invoice design or template used, e.g. standard.

currency

string

Currency used for the invoice.

issueDate

string

Date the invoice was created, formatted as YYYY-MM-DD.

dueDate

string

Invoice payment due date, formatted as YYYY-MM-DD.

items

array

Invoice line items (see LINE_ITEM).

taxRate

number

Applicable tax percentage.

shipping

number

Shipping amount. Stored in the document but not currently used in the invoice form.

subtotal

number

Sum of all invoice line item amounts before tax and shipping.

tax

number

Calculated tax amount.

total

number

Final invoice amount due.

payment

map

Payment information, including type (link or bank), link, and bank (copy of BANK).

extra

map

Optional invoice subject and reference information.

notes

string

Additional notes or instructions for the client.

status

string

Invoice status: SAVED, SENT, or PAID.

sentAt

timestamp

Timestamp indicating when the invoice was emailed, generated using Firebase server time.

paidAt

timestamp

Timestamp indicating when the invoice was marked as paid, generated using Firebase server time.

createdAt

timestamp

Timestamp indicating when the invoice document was created.

updatedAt

timestamp

Timestamp indicating when the invoice was last updated.

LINE_ITEM (each entry in the items array)

Each invoice contains an items array representing the individual products or services being billed to the client. Each entry follows this structure:

Field

Type

Description

id

string

Unique identifier for the line item.

description

string

Description of the product or service delivered.

details

string

Optional additional information about the item.

quantity

number

Quantity of items or number of hours billed.

rate

number

Price per unit. The line item amount is calculated as quantity × rate.

Using this data structure, each invoice is assigned a sequential number (seq) when it is created. This allows the application to generate unique invoice numbers, such as INV-001, INV-002, and INV-003.

The clientOrderNumber field also maintains a separate sequence for each client, making it easier to identify and organise the invoices issued to a particular customer.

Managing invoice statuses

Each invoice has a status field that tracks its progress through the invoicing process:

  • SAVED: created and saved but has not yet been emailed to the client.
  • SENT: sent to the client’s email address through the application.
  • PAID: marked as paid by the business.

An invoice can also become OVERDUE when its payment due date has passed without being marked as paid. Unlike the other statuses, OVERDUE is calculated from the invoice’s dueDate and current payment status rather than stored directly in the status field.

When a user marks an invoice as paid, its status changes to PAID, and the paidAt field is updated with the corresponding timestamp.

Build an Invoice App with Claude Code

In this section, I’ll walk you through how to use Claude Code to build the invoicing application using a detailed prompt. The prompt covers the application’s architecture, user interface, Firebase integration, invoice management features, and email functionality.

Before we proceed, make sure you have Claude Desktop installed and configured on your computer. You’ll also need a Claude Pro subscription or higher to access Claude Code with the appropriate usage limits for this workflow.

Install Firebase CLI

First, install the Firebase CLI globally on your computer using the following command:

npm install -g firebase-tools

The Firebase CLI allows you to interact with your Firebase projects from the terminal. We’ll use it to authenticate with Firebase and manage the project’s Firebase services during development.

Next, sign in to your Google account using the following command:

firebase login

If you’ve previously authenticated and want to refresh your login credentials, you can use:

firebase login --reauth

Once you’ve successfully signed in, you should see a confirmation message similar to the one below:

Build the application with Claude Code

Now that Claude Code and Firebase CLI are ready, you can now build the application.

Copy the prompts below into Claude Code to guide it through building the invoicing application, from the initial project setup to Firebase integration and implementation of its core features.

## TASK/DESIGN:

I want you to build a modern, highly interactive invoicing application website for businesses and freelancers using Next.js, TypeScript, and Firebase, with a sleek user interface and smooth, engaging animations. Ensure that all pages are mobile-friendly and responsive across different screen sizes.

The website should be production-ready, fully interactive, and user-friendly. Before writing any code, show me the designs for each page and wait for my approval before proceeding with the implementation.

**You must present the designs first. I must approve them or request changes before you start writing any code.**

## PAGES:

- `/` - A modern homepage with 5–7 sections, featuring engaging animations and strategically placed call-to-action buttons to convert visitors into users.
- `/register` - User registration page supporting Google and Email/Password authentication.
- `/login` - User sign-in page.
- `/business/setup` - Business setup page where users can provide their business information, upload their business logo, and configure other relevant details.
- `/dashboard` - Main dashboard for managing customers, invoices, and payments.
- Other pages as required to support the application's functionality.

## ROLES and PERMISSIONS:

Businesses should be able to add customers and create, read, update, and delete invoices associated with their customers.

Businesses should also be able to send invoices as printable PDF attachments directly to their customers' email addresses using

- jsPDF
- Zernio Email API: https://docs.zernio.com/products/email

## CODE STRUCTURE

- Use a `components` folder to organise reusable page components and individual page sections.
- Import and reference these components within their respective pages.
- Store images in an `images` folder at the root of the project. Use high-quality images wherever necessary.
- Follow the DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) principle to maintain clean, reusable, and readable code.
- Create a `firebase.ts` file and a `firebase-actions` file to organise Firebase configuration and the various operations required to handle application data securely and efficiently.
- You can also create a `styles` folder for reusable styles.

Congratulations! You’ve successfully built your invoicing application. Check out the live demo to see it in action and explore the source code on GitHub.

Conclusion

In this tutorial, you’ve learnt how to build a modern, full-stack invoicing application using Next.js, TypeScript, Firebase, and Claude Code. You’ve also explored how to structure your Firestore database, implement user authentication, manage customers and invoices, generate printable PDF invoices, and send them directly to clients’ email addresses using the Zernio Email API.

With well-structured prompts and clear technical requirements, developers can use AI coding agents to plan application architecture, generate components, integrate backend services, implement features, and debug code. Rather than replacing the developer’s understanding of software engineering, these tools can accelerate development and help turn ideas into functional software products.

If you’d like to explore these technologies further, here are some helpful resources worth reading:

  • Frontend to FullStack: Introduction to Firebase (Firebase v9)
  • Build an Invoice Management System Using React & Firebase v9
  • How to Build an AI Social Media Post Scheduler Using Gemini and Zernio API in Next.js
  • Full Stack Software Development Projects

Thank you for reading!
