articles.description: Why double charges happen, the exact contract that prevents them, and working code you can adapt.  A...
articles.body_html:
Why double charges happen, the exact contract that prevents them, and working code you can adapt.

A customer taps “Pay.” The request reaches your server, the payment is recorded, but the response is lost on a flaky mobile connection. The app times out and retries. Your server sees a brand new request and charges the customer again.

This is one of the most common API design interview questions, and one of the most common production bugs. The fix is a small idea called an idempotency key. In this post you will learn the contract, then build a working version with PostgreSQL and Python.

Idempotent, in One Sentence

An operation is idempotent if doing it many times has the same effect as doing it once.

In HTTP, GET, PUT and DELETE are meant to be idempotent. POST is not, because posting twice usually creates two things. Payments, orders and transfers are almost always POSTs, so they need extra protection.

The Contract

The client generates a unique key (a UUID works well) for each logical operation and sends it in a header:

POST /payments
Idempotency-Key: 4d7a6c1e-9f0b-4f6e-8a55-1c2d3e4f5a6b
Content-Type: application/json

{"customer_id": 17, "amount_cents": 2000, "currency": "usd"}

The server then follows these rules:

1.First time this key is seen: Do the work, save the result with the key, and return it.

2.Same key, same request body: Do not repeat the work; return the saved result.

3.Same key, different request body: Reject with 422.

4.Same key while the first request is still running: Wait for it, or return 409 Conflict.

The client reuses the same key on every retry of the same action, and creates a new key for each new action.

The Table

We store each key together with a fingerprint of the request and the saved response:

CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  key           TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  request_hash  TEXT NOT NULL,
  response_code INT,
  response_body JSONB,
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE payments (
  id           BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id  BIGINT NOT NULL,
  amount_cents INT NOT NULL CHECK (amount_cents > 0),
  currency     CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
  created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

The PRIMARY KEY on key does the hard part for us: the database itself guarantees that a key can only be inserted once, even if two requests arrive at the same instant.

The Handler
Here is the core logic using psycopg2. The key trick is to claim the key and do the work inside one transaction.

import hashlib
import json

def create_payment(conn, idem_key, payload):
    request_hash = hashlib.sha256(
        json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True).encode()
    ).hexdigest()

    with conn:                       # one transaction: commit on success, rollback on error
        with conn.cursor() as cur:
            # 1. Try to claim the key.
            cur.execute(
                """INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (key, request_hash)
                   VALUES (%s, %s)
                   ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING
                   RETURNING key""",
                (idem_key, request_hash),
            )

            if cur.fetchone() is None:
                # 2. Key already used: replay or reject.
                cur.execute(
                    "SELECT request_hash, response_code, response_body "
                    "FROM idempotency_keys WHERE key = %s",
                    (idem_key,),
                )
                saved_hash, code, body = cur.fetchone()
                if saved_hash != request_hash:
                    return 422, {"error": "Idempotency-Key reused with a different request"}
                return code, body

            # 3. First time: do the real work.
            cur.execute(
                "INSERT INTO payments (customer_id, amount_cents, currency) "
                "VALUES (%s, %s, %s) RETURNING id",
                (payload["customer_id"], payload["amount_cents"], payload["currency"]),
            )
            payment_id = cur.fetchone()[0]
            response = {"payment_id": payment_id, "status": "succeeded"}

            # 4. Save the response with the key.
            cur.execute(
                "UPDATE idempotency_keys SET response_code = 201, response_body = %s "
                "WHERE key = %s",
                (json.dumps(response), idem_key),
            )
            return 201, response

What Happens When You Call It Twice

create_payment(conn, "4d7a...", {...})  ->  (201, {"payment_id": 1, "status": "succeeded"})
create_payment(conn, "4d7a...", {...})  ->  (201, {"payment_id": 1, "status": "succeeded"})   # replayed, no new row
create_payment(conn, "4d7a...", {amount changed})  ->  (422, {"error": "...reused..."})

The payments table has exactly one row. The retry got the original answer back.

The Subtle Case: Two Requests at the Same Moment

Suppose the client’s retry arrives while the first request is still running. Because both try to insert the same primary key, PostgreSQL makes the second INSERT ... ON CONFLICT wait until the first transaction finishes. When the first commits, the second hits the conflict, does nothing, reads the saved response and replays it. If the first transaction fails and rolls back, the second one proceeds normally. No double charge, and no extra locking code.

A Real Gotcha: Calling an External Payment Provider

The example above works because the “work” is a database write. If your work calls an external provider, you should not hold a database transaction open during a slow network call. The usual approach is:

  1. Insert the key with a status of in_progress and commit.
  2. Call the provider, passing your own idempotency key along so it is also protected.
  3. Update the key with the final response and set the status to completed.
  4. If a retry arrives while the status is in_progress, return 409 Conflict (and tell the client to retry shortly).
  5. Run a recovery job for keys stuck in_progress for too long.

Don’t Forget the Client

The server is only half of the contract. A good client:
• Generates the key once per user action and reuses it for every retry of that action.
• Retries only when it makes sense: network errors, timeouts, 5xx and 429.
• Uses exponential backoff with jitter, so thousands of clients do not retry at the same instant.

Housekeeping

• Expire old keys. Keeping them forever grows the table. Many APIs keep them for a limited window (for example, 24 hours) and delete older ones with a scheduled job. Document the window for your clients.
• Decide what to store. Saving the outcome of every completed request keeps replays consistent. Let genuinely transient failures (a 503) be retried instead of cached.
• Index and size. The primary key is the only index you need for the lookup.

How to Say This in an Interview (45 Seconds)

“Retries after a timeout can double-charge a customer, because POST is not idempotent. I would require an Idempotency-Key header, a unique ID the client generates per action. On the server I store the key with a hash of the request and the saved response, with a unique constraint so concurrent attempts cannot both succeed. A repeat with the same key and body returns the saved response, the same key with a different body gets a 422, and a request still in progress gets a 409. I would expire keys after a window like 24 hours, and if I call an external provider, I would pass the key through to it.”

Common Mistakes

• Using GET or a database row count as a “double-click guard” instead of a real key.
• Generating a new key on each retry (which defeats the purpose).
• Not comparing the request body, so a reused key silently does the wrong thing.
• Holding a database transaction open while calling an external API.
• Forgetting to expire keys.

Keep Practising API Design

Idempotency is just one of the “hard parts” of API design interviews, alongside pagination, versioning, errors and rate limits. If you want to practise designing and defending APIs hands-on, the API Design Lab on ScaleDojo has 144 levels, and you can start for free.

articles.title: I Built an AI Loop That Finds "Lost My Work" Bugs and Fixes Them Until the Test Passes
articles.description: Kane CLI tests in a real browser, Codex repairs the code, and the same test runs again until it passes.
articles.body_html:
We've all done it. You fill in a long sign-up form, a job application, or a checkout, press Back or Refresh, and everything you typed is gone. These "lost my work" bugs are everywhere, and unit tests rarely catch them because they only show up in a real browser.

For the KaneCLI Online Hackathon by TestMu AI, I built StillHere: a loop that catches these bugs in a real browser and keeps fixing them until the test passes.

What it does

StillHere runs a closed loop:

  1. Find it. Kane CLI drives a real Chrome session through a journey described in plain English: fill in a checkout, open another page, press Back, press Refresh, and check the cart, details, and current step are still there.
  2. Fix it. If anything is wiped, Kane's failure report becomes a repair prompt for the Codex coding agent, which fixes the app without weakening the test.
  3. Prove it. The exact same Kane objective re-runs, unchanged, until it passes.

It works for any form or multi-step flow via --objective, not just checkout.

How I built it

Node.js with no dependencies. StillHere calls Kane CLI with --agent, parses its NDJSON result, writes a failure report with evidence and screenshots, and pipes a repair prompt to codex exec. A sample shop with a real Back/Refresh bug is included, and npm run demo:loop resets the bug so you always see fail, fix, pass. Built solo with Codex.

What Kane caught

In the recorded run, pressing "Back to checkout" wiped the order: the cart, the customer's details, and the review step were all gone. Codex fixed it by saving state in sessionStorage plus browser history and restoring it on load and Back. Kane then passed through both Back and Refresh. The test was never changed to make it pass.

Challenges

Chrome crashed when launched from a sandbox, so Kane runs from a normal terminal. Long Kane runs timed out, so the default timeout became 300 seconds. I also made sure a run with no final Kane result counts as incomplete, not as a failure for the agent to "fix."

What I learned

Verifying in a real browser catches bugs a mock never would, and keeping the test fixed is what makes an AI fix trustworthy.

What's next

A GitHub Action that runs the loop on every pull request, plus ready-made objectives for sign-up, login, and multi-step forms.

Try it

  • Code and setup: https://github.com/Mzee04/stillhere
  • Demo: https://youtu.be/4R3yvR5oKvg

What "lost my work" bugs have you run into?

articles.title: I built shadcn/ui for Angular 22: install it or own the source
articles.description: Ivorie: 54 Angular components with the shadcn/ui look. Signals, zoneless, SSR, Tailwind 4. An npm package, or a CLI that copies the code into your app.
articles.body_html:
React developers have had shadcn/ui for a while: good-looking components, accessible by default, and code you own. I work in Angular, and I wanted the same thing for Angular. Same classes, same variants, same feel, and current Angular, not something ported from an older version.

I couldn't find a close match, so I built it. It's called Ivorie, it's MIT, and version 1.5.2 is on npm today.

This post shows what it does with real code you can paste.

  • Repo: https://github.com/Inlaylab/ivorie
  • Docs and playground: https://inlaylab.github.io/ivorie/

Ivorie is an independent project. It's not affiliated with shadcn/ui. It ports shadcn/ui's design (MIT) to Angular, with credit.

What you get

  • 54 components with the shadcn/ui look and behavior. Keyboard and ARIA follow Radix patterns.
  • Angular 22 only. Signal inputs, model(), zoneless, SSR. It also works in NgModule apps.
  • Tailwind CSS 4.
  • Two ways in. Install @inlaylab/ivorie from npm and get updates. Or run the ivorie CLI, which copies the source into your app so you can edit it.
  • 13 styles (shadcn's eight plus glass, bento, mono, graphite and tint), 7 base colors, 17 accent colors, 26 fonts, 5 radius options.
  • 5 icon libraries: Lucide, Tabler, Phosphor, Hugeicons, Remix.
  • A data table with sort, pagination, filter, selection and column visibility. It runs in the browser or against your API.
  • 22 blocks: login, sign-up, sidebar and dashboard pages, already wired.

Path 1: the npm package 

npm i @inlaylab/ivorie @angular/cdk @lucide/angular
npm i -D tailwindcss @tailwindcss/postcss tw-animate-css

/* src/styles.css */
@import "@inlaylab/ivorie/styles/theme.css";
@import "@inlaylab/ivorie/styles/style-nova.css";

Add class="style-nova" to <body>. Then import only what you use. Each component has its own entry point, so your bundle carries only those:

import { Component } from '@angular/core';
import { IvButton } from '@inlaylab/ivorie/button';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-root',
  imports: [IvButton],
  template: `<button ivButton>Save</button>`,
})
export class App {}

The full setup, with the Tailwind config, is on the Installation page.

Path 2: copy the source and own it

This is the shadcn way. The code lands in your repo. Change anything.

npx ivorie init
npx ivorie add button dialog

init sets up the theme, the style and components.json. add copies components to src/app/ui by default (--path changes that). You can even pick your own selector prefix with --prefix.

Both paths come from one source. The CLI copies from the same library code that npm ships, so they don't drift apart.

A sortable table in 30 lines

The data table isn't one big component. It's five small features: ivSort, ivFilter, ivPagination, ivRowSelection and ivColumnVisibility. Rows go in and rows come out, as signals. Use one, or all five. The cells stay in your template.

Here's sorting on its own:

import { ChangeDetectionStrategy, Component, signal } from '@angular/core';
import { IV_DATA_TABLE_IMPORTS, IvColumnDef, ivSort } from '@inlaylab/ivorie/data-table';

interface Release { version: string; name: string; }

const RELEASES: Release[] = [
  { version: '1.2.0', name: 'Playground' },
  { version: '1.10.0', name: 'Later work' },
  { version: '1.0.0', name: 'First release' },
];

const COLUMNS: IvColumnDef<Release>[] = [
  { id: 'version', header: 'Version', accessor: (r) => r.version, sortable: true },
  { id: 'name', header: 'Name', accessor: (r) => r.name, sortable: true },
];

@Component({
  selector: 'app-releases',
  imports: [IV_DATA_TABLE_IMPORTS],
  changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush,
  template: `
    <iv-table class="rounded-lg border">
      <thead ivTableHeader>
        <tr ivTableRow>
          @for (c of columns; track c.id) {
            <th [ivDataTableSort]="c.id" [sort]="sort">{{ c.header }}</th>
          }
        </tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody ivTableBody>
        @for (r of sort.rows(); track r.version) {
          <tr ivTableRow>
            <td ivTableCell class="font-mono">{{ r.version }}</td>
            <td ivTableCell>{{ r.name }}</td>
          </tr>
        }
      </tbody>
    </iv-table>
  `,
})
export class Releases {
  protected readonly columns = COLUMNS;
  protected readonly sort = ivSort(signal(RELEASES), {
    columns: COLUMNS,
    initial: { id: 'version', desc: false },
  });
}

The sort header sets aria-sort and works with the keyboard. Versions sort as numbers, so 1.10.0 comes after 1.2.0.

Server mode

When the data lives on your server, switch to mode: 'server'. The table stops sorting and paging in the browser. Instead it gives you one query() signal with the page, sort and filter. Feed that to resource() or httpResource():

protected readonly table: IvDataTable<Order> = ivDataTable<Order>({
  mode: 'server',
  data: computed(() => this.page().rows),
  rowCount: computed(() => this.page().total),
  columns: COLUMNS,
  getRowId: (o) => String(o.id),
  pageSize: 5,
});

protected readonly orders = resource<OrderPage, IvDataTableQuery>({
  params: () => this.table.query(),
  loader: ({ params, abortSignal }) => fetchOrders(params, abortSignal),
});

It's the same API in both modes. The full example, with the loading and empty rows, is on the data table page.

A login page in one command

Blocks are whole pages. They're wired, not just markup: reactive forms with validation, typed outputs, and pending and error inputs.

npx ivorie add login-01

This writes the page to src/app/blocks/login-01/. It also adds the components the page needs, fixes the imports, and renames the icons to your icon library. All that's left is your auth call:

@Component({
  selector: 'app-login-01',
  imports: [LoginForm],
  template: `
    <div class="w-full max-w-sm">
      <app-login-01-form (submitted)="login($event)" (provider)="loginWith($event)" />
    </div>
  `,
})
export class Login01 {
  protected login(value: LoginValue): void {
    // Call your auth API here, then navigate.
  }

  protected loginWith(provider: 'google' | 'github' | 'apple'): void {
    // Start your OAuth flow here.
  }
}

There are 22 blocks: five logins, five sign-ups, eight sidebars and four dashboards. See them live at /blocks.

Make it look like your product

Open the playground. Pick a style, base color, font, heading font, radius and icon library. Real components update as you click. Then copy one command:

# new app
npx ivorie init --preset ivp1_…

# existing app: change the whole look
npx ivorie apply ivp1_…

The ivp1_… code holds your whole look, so you can share it with your team or paste it in an issue. Flags work too:

npx ivorie init --style glass --base-color zinc --radius large --icon-library tabler

Changing icon libraries later? npx ivorie migrate icons --from lucide --to tabler renames the icons in your own templates as well.

A note on the new styles: glass uses backdrop-filter. Where that isn't supported, or the user asks for reduced transparency, it turns solid. Every style has a test that checks text contrast (4.5:1 or more) for every base color, in light and dark mode.

How it's built

A few choices you may care about:

  • Signals all the way down. input(), model(), output(), computed(). No @Input() decorators. A lint rule blocks them.
  • No @angular/animations. Motion is CSS through tw-animate-css.
  • SSR is tested on every change. The docs app is server-rendered, and a smoke test loads every page in a real browser.
  • One command for every gate. npm run check runs every build, the unit specs (Vitest, with axe for accessibility), SSR, the package and CLI tests, and the lint rules.
  • The registry uses the shadcn registry JSON format.
  • Releases carry npm provenance and are published from GitHub Actions.

What's next, and how you can help

  • 1.6: more theme dials: density, and how much glass.
  • 1.7: AI-ready. An AGENTS.md that ivorie init writes, llms.txt for the docs, and an MCP server so coding agents can browse and add components.

I'd love help with these, and with the smaller issues labeled good first issue. There are new blocks to build, CLI commands like ivorie list and ivorie diff, and docs search. Read CONTRIBUTING.md, run npm install && npm run check, and you're set.

If you try it, tell me what broke or what you missed. Issues are the most useful thing you can give a new library. If it saves you time, a star on GitHub helps other Angular devs find it.

Thanks for reading.

articles.title: My Feather Fractal Was Just Two Blobs: Fixing 2 Rational Dynamics Bugs in WebGL & NumPy
articles.description: How a missing imaginary unit turned the Feather fractal into smooth blobs, and an unanchored critical value scrambled the Nova fractal in WebGL & NumPy.
articles.body_html:
My Feather Fractal Was Just Two Blobs: Fixing 2 Rational Dynamics Bugs in WebGL & NumPy

🔗 Quick Links

  • 🚀 Live Demo (60 FPS WebGL 2.0): https://fantasticfractals.pages.dev
  • ⭐ GitHub (MIT Open Source): https://github.com/QuantumTechCoder/FantasticFractals
  • 📦 PyPI: pip install fantasticfractals → https://pypi.org/project/fantasticfractals/
  • 📓 1-Click Google Colab: Open in Colab

Right after fixing the Sierpinski gothic arch and Koch snowflake slider bugs on FantasticFractals, I thought our 27 fractal formulas were finally rock solid.

Then user testing struck again.

Someone dropped two side-by-side screenshots into our issues:

  1. "Why does the Feather Fractal look like two smooth horizontal blobs? When I search Google Images, feather fractals have organic plume filaments."
  2. "What's wrong with the Nova Fractal? It looks like a 3-lobed bullseye instead of the iconic Paul Derbyshire crescent."

I opened Google Images, compared their search results against my WebGL canvas, and realized I had completely botched the complex rational math for both systems.

Here is the breakdown of what broke, why complex phase twists matter, and how we fixed both fractals in GLSL and NumPy.

Bug #1: The "Two Smooth Blobs" Feather Fractal 🪶

Here is what FantasticFractals was rendering when you selected the Feather Fractal:

It was literally two giant, smooth cyan circles with a central black oval. No plumes. No barbs. Zero feather-like structure.

The Math Mistake: $1 + z^2$ vs $1 + i|z|^2$

In my original code, I had implemented this formula:
$$z_{n+1} = rac{z_n^3}{1 + z_n^2} + c$$

// ❌ WRONG FORMULA:
vec2 z2 = vec2(z.x * z.x - z.y * z.y, 2.0 * z.x * z.y);
vec2 denom = vec2(1.0 + z2.x, z2.y); // <-- Standard complex 1 + z^2

Because $1 + z^2$ has real coefficients, the denominator is analytic and preserves standard bilateral symmetry. Near the origin, it just behaves like $z^3 + c$, which produces smooth, rounded cardioid lobes.

The Real Formula from Mandelbrowser

The authentic Feather Fractal (popularized by Mandelbrowser and fractal art forums) uses an imaginary phase coupling in the denominator:

$$z_{n+1} = rac{z_n^3}{1 + i |z_n|^2} + c$$

Look closely at that denominator:
$$ ext{denom} = 1 + i(x^2 + y^2)$$

It uses the Euclidean magnitude squared $|z|^2 = x^2 + y^2$, multiplied by the imaginary unit $i$!

Why this creates the "Feather" effect:

Because $|z|^2$ is purely real, multiplying it by $i$ forces the denominator to rotate the phase of $z^3$ by an angle that dynamically increases with distance from the origin:
$$ heta_{ ext{twist}} = -rctan(|z|^2)$$

This nonlinear phase rotation shears the escape trajectories, pulling the boundaries into razor-thin, dendritic plume filaments that burst outward along the diagonals.

The Fix in GLSL: 

// ✅ THE FIX:
vec2 z = vec2(0.0);
int i = 0;
for (; i < 500; i++) {
  if (i >= u_maxIterations) break;
  float r2 = dot(z, z);
  if (r2 > 16.0) {
    // Continuous potential shading
    float log_zn = log(r2) / 2.0;
    float nu = log(max(1.0, log_zn) / 0.693147) / 0.693147;
    iterVal = float(i) + 1.0 - nu;
    break;
  }
  // z^3 = (x^3 - 3xy^2) + i(3x^2y - y^3)
  vec2 z3 = vec2(z.x * (z.x * z.x - 3.0 * z.y * z.y), z.y * (3.0 * z.x * z.x - z.y * z.y));

  // denom = 1 + i*|z|^2 -> divide by (1 + i*r2)
  float denNorm = 1.0 + r2 * r2;
  vec2 frac = vec2(z3.x + z3.y * r2, z3.y - z3.x * r2) / denNorm;
  z = frac + c;
}

Here is the exact same coordinate plane after deploying the fix:

Now it actually looks like an explosive plumage of organic fractal feathers.

Bug #2: The "Concentric Bullseye" Nova Fractal 🌟

The second bug was in our Nova Fractal. Here is what was on screen:

A symmetric 3-petaled blob surrounded by concentric bullseye rings.

If you search Wikipedia or Ultra Fractal for the Nova fractal, you don't see a bullseye—you see an iconic crescent-shaped central bay with intricate Mandelbrot filaments and satellite islands wrapping around its rim.

What Caused This?

Paul Derbyshire invented the Nova fractal in 1997 by taking the classic Newton-Raphson root-finding method for $f(z) = z^3 - 1$:
$$z_{n+1} = z_n - R rac{z^3 - 1}{3z^2}$$

And adding the coordinate $c$ at each step (with standard relaxation $R = 1$):
$$z_{n+1} = rac{2z_n + rac{1}{z_n^2}}{3} + c$$

My implementation had three distinct bugs:

  1. Incorrect Critical Initialization ($z_0$):
    I had initialized $z_0 = c$. But in the canonical Mandelbrot formulation of the Nova fractal, the iteration must start at the critical root anchor $z_0 = 1.0$ ($1 + 0i$)!
    Starting at $z_0 = c$ scrambles the parameter dynamics into an arbitrary slice, collapsing the crescent.

  2. Accidental Coordinate Dampening:
    In my shader, someone had written:

   vec2 nextZ = (2.0 * z + invZ2) / 3.0 + c * 0.2; // ❌ WHY * 0.2?!

Dampening $c$ by $0.2$ suppressed the chaotic perturbation, causing the Newton basins to dominate and form concentric rings.

  1. Wrong Default Center & Zoom: The center was hardcoded at (0.0, 0.0). But because $z_0 = 1$, the main crescent of the Nova Mandelbrot set is centered near $x pprox -0.5, y = 0.0$.

The Fix in GLSL: 

// ✅ THE FIX:
vec2 z = vec2(1.0, 0.0); // Canonical critical anchor z0 = 1
int i = 0;
for (; i < 500; i++) {
  if (i >= u_maxIterations) break;
  float d2 = dot(z, z);
  if (d2 < 1e-8) break;

  // 1 / z^2
  float invD4 = 1.0 / (d2 * d2);
  vec2 invZ2 = vec2(z.x * z.x - z.y * z.y, -2.0 * z.x * z.y) * invD4;

  // Full c addition: (2z + 1/z^2)/3 + c
  vec2 nextZ = (2.0 * z + invZ2) / 3.0 + c;

  // Convergence check to fixed point:
  vec2 diff = nextZ - z;
  if (dot(diff, diff) < 1e-7) {
    iterVal = float(i) * 2.5;
    break;
  }
  // Divergence check:
  if (dot(nextZ, nextZ) > 100.0) {
    iterVal = float(i) * 2.5 + 50.0;
    break;
  }
  z = nextZ;
}

And centering the camera at defaultCenter: { x: -0.5, y: 0.0 }.

Here is the corrected Nova Fractal:

The authentic Paul Derbyshire crescent with its necklace of satellite Mandelbrot sets and delicate tendrils is fully restored.

Keeping NumPy Vectorization Synchronized 🐍

Because FantasticFractals is also a published Python scientific package (pip install fantasticfractals), fixing the WebGL shaders meant updating the vectorized NumPy array kernels as well.

Here is the NumPy vectorized kernel for the fixed Feather Fractal:

# Vectorized Feather Fractal in NumPy:
Z = np.zeros(C.shape, dtype=complex)
iters = np.full(C.shape, -1.0, dtype=np.float64)
active = np.ones(C.shape, dtype=bool)

for i in range(max_iterations):
    if not np.any(active):
        break
    z_act = Z[active]
    c_act = C[active]

    r2 = z_act.real**2 + z_act.imag**2
    escaped = r2 > 16.0

    if np.any(escaped):
        act_idx = np.where(active)[0][escaped], np.where(active)[1][escaped]
        r2_esc = r2[escaped]
        log_zn = np.log(r2_esc) / 2.0
        nu = np.log2(np.maximum(1.0, log_zn))
        iters[act_idx] = float(i) + 1.0 - nu
        active[act_idx] = False

    z_rem = z_act[~escaped]
    c_rem = c_act[~escaped]
    r2_rem = r2[~escaped]

    # Authentic 1 + i*|z|^2 denominator
    denom = 1.0 + 1j * r2_rem
    Z[active] = (z_rem ** 3) / denom + c_rem

Both client-side GPU shaders and Python library functions now produce identical mathematical outputs down to floating-point precision.

Key Lessons

  1. Phase matters: If a fractal formula contains $i$ in the denominator (like $1 + i|z|^2$), you cannot treat it as a standard real polynomial. That imaginary unit is doing the heavy lifting of twisting coordinate space into fractal plumes.
  2. Critical values anchor parameter spaces: For Newton-type relaxation fractals like Nova, starting at $z_0 = c$ versus $z_0 = 1$ is the difference between a blurry bullseye and the true Mandelbrot crescent.
  3. Always visually cross-reference fractal literature: Unit tests can pass, but if you don't visually cross-reference against original papers or historical fractal databases, you can easily end up with smooth blobs pretending to be fractals.

Check Out the Fixes Live

Everything is pushed and deployed:

  • 🌐 Live Web Visualizer: https://fantasticfractals.pages.dev
  • ⭐ GitHub (MIT): https://github.com/QuantumTechCoder/FantasticFractals
  • 📦 PyPI: pip install fantasticfractals
  • 📓 Colab: Open in Google Colab

What's the weirdest bug you've ever encountered in numerical or shader math? Share your stories below! 👇

articles.title: Show DEV: Monetizing an Open Source WebRTC App Without Stripe, Subscriptions, or Paywalls (Part 2)
articles.description: How I built an on-chain, zero-trust micropayment and licensing engine with USDC on Base and Polygon—keeping P2P free forever while selling TURN relay passes and enterprise white-labeling.
articles.body_html:
TL;DR

🚀 Live Web App (Free, No Signup): air-stream.pages.dev

⭐ GitHub Repo (MIT): github.com/QuantumTechCoder/AirStream

📖 Missed Part 1? Catch up here: Show DEV: AirStream — Stream Gigabytes Browser-to-Browser with WebRTC (No Cloud, No Size Limits)

The Indie Hacker's Worst Dilemma

In Part 1 of this series, I shared how I built AirStream—an open-source PWA that opens encrypted, direct browser-to-browser data tunnels using WebRTC RTCDataChannel, letting people stream 10GB+ files at gigabit Wi-Fi speeds without cloud servers or size caps.

The feedback was incredible. But within 48 hours of launching, I hit the universal wall that every open-source builder eventually crashes into:

  1. Bandwidth isn't 100% free when firewalls get aggressive. Standard STUN traversal handles ~85–90% of home networks. But users on strict corporate firewalls, university Wi-Fi, and symmetric mobile cellular NATs (like Reliance Jio or AT&T) require TURN relay fallback servers. High-bandwidth TURN relays cost real money to maintain.
  2. I despise aggressive SaaS paywalls. Slapping a 2GB cap, forcing user registrations, or putting intrusive Google Ad banners on a clean privacy-first tool destroys everything that makes open-source great.
  3. Traditional payment processors (Stripe, PayPal) are terrible for lightweight indie apps.

So I asked myself: How can I keep AirStream 100% free and open-source forever, while creating ethical, frictionless revenue streams that actually respect user privacy?

Here is the story of how I designed an on-chain, zero-trust micropayment architecture powered by USDC on Base and Polygon—and why web3 stablecoins turned out to be the ultimate indie monetization rail.

Why Traditional Payment Rails Failed

When considering payments for an open-source tool, traditional options like Stripe or Lemonsqueezy seem like the default choice. But for AirStream, they created massive architectural friction:

  • 💸 The Flat-Fee Trap: Stripe charges roughly \$0.30 + 2.9% per transaction. If someone transfers a 30GB video file and wants to send a \$1 or \$2 tip to say "thanks for saving my evening," 35% to 40% of their tip gets vaporized by processing fees.
  • 🌐 Global Friction & KYC Walls: A huge portion of our users are developers, video editors, and students in India, Latin America, Southeast Asia, and Eastern Europe. Stripe Checkout often rejects international cards or requires phone numbers, postal codes, and 3D-Secure redirects.
  • 🗄️ Database & Auth Bloat: To verify paid subscriptions with Stripe Webhooks, I would have had to spin up a PostgreSQL database, write authentication logic (JWTs / OAuth), and store user emails. AirStream has zero logins, zero databases, and zero user telemetry. Introducing accounts just to process payments felt backwards.

The Architecture: Zero-Trust On-Chain USDC (Base & Polygon)

Instead of traditional merchant processors, I implemented native USDC payments on Layer-2 networks (Base and Polygon).

Why Base and Polygon?

  1. Negligible Gas Fees: Transferring USDC on Base or Polygon costs under \$0.01 (often \$0.003–\$0.005).
  2. Stable Currency: USDC is pegged 1:1 to the US Dollar—no crypto price volatility for either the user or the developer.
  3. Decentralized Verification: No backend database needed. The blockchain is an immutable public ledger. The client app can verify payments directly against decentralized RPC nodes!

Maximum Security: Preventing Spoofed Payments

One of the biggest requirements was: Make sure no one can fake payments or forge transactions.

In a client-side web application, you cannot just trust a frontend input box that says "I paid! Here's a transaction hash." An attacker could try to:

  • Paste a random transaction hash from an unrelated transfer.
  • Paste a failed or reverted transaction.
  • Paste a real transaction sent to someone else's wallet.
  • Send 0.000001 USDC and claim a 30 USDC license.
  • Reuse an old transaction hash from another user.

To make the verification 100% zero-trust, I engineered an on-chain validator in TypeScript that inspects the raw EVM transaction receipts via decentralized JSON-RPC nodes:

// src/utils/paymentVerifier.ts
export async function verifyOnChainPayment(
  txHash: string,
  expectedChain: SupportedChain,
  minUsdcAmount: number
): Promise<VerificationResult> {
  const cleanHash = txHash.trim();

  // 1. Verify 64-character hex format
  if (!/^0x([A-Fa-f0-9]{64})$/.test(cleanHash)) {
    return { valid: false, error: 'Invalid transaction hash format.' };
  }

  // 2. Fetch immutable transaction receipt directly from RPC
  const receipt = await rpcCall(expectedChain, 'eth_getTransactionReceipt', [cleanHash]);
  if (!receipt) {
    return { valid: false, error: 'Transaction still pending in mempool.' };
  }

  // 3. Ensure the transaction actually succeeded (status 0x1)
  if (receipt.status !== '0x1') {
    return { valid: false, error: 'Transaction was reverted on-chain.' };
  }

  const recipientNormalized = RECIPIENT_WALLET.toLowerCase();
  const network = NETWORKS[expectedChain];
  let isMatched = false;
  let matchedUsdcAmount = 0;

  // 4. Parse raw EVM event logs for ERC-20 Transfer
  if (Array.isArray(receipt.logs)) {
    for (const log of receipt.logs) {
      const contract = (log.address || '').toLowerCase();
      const isUsdc = contract === network.usdcAddress.toLowerCase();

      // Topic 0: Transfer(address,address,uint256) signature
      if (isUsdc && log.topics && log.topics[0] === TRANSFER_TOPIC) {
        // Topic 2: Recipient address (padded to 32 bytes)
        const toAddress = '0x' + log.topics[2].slice(26).toLowerCase();

        if (toAddress === recipientNormalized) {
          const rawValue = BigInt(log.data);
          const actualAmount = Number(rawValue) / Math.pow(10, network.usdcDecimals);

          // Verify exact expected amount (with 1% micro-rounding tolerance)
          if (actualAmount >= minUsdcAmount * 0.99) {
            matchedUsdcAmount = actualAmount;
            isMatched = true;
            break;
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }

  if (!isMatched) {
    return { valid: false, error: 'No matching USDC payment found in this receipt.' };
  }

  return { valid: true, txHash: cleanHash, amount: matchedUsdcAmount };
}

How this guarantees cryptographic security:

  • Receipt Status: If a transaction reverted or threw an out-of-gas error, receipt.status !== '0x1' rejects it.
  • Contract Address Matching: Only official USDC contract addresses (0x833589... on Base, 0x3c499c... on Polygon) are parsed. Custom fake ERC-20 tokens are ignored.
  • Topic Decoding: Decodes the padded 32-byte to address to ensure funds actually arrived at developer address 0x2cef0473f985156eDe84312Ce0BeB94B602d26E4.
  • Decimal Precision: Computes the exact integer value divided by $10^6$ (USDC decimals) to ensure the full amount was paid.

The Sustainable Monetization Pillars

With zero-trust on-chain verification in place, I introduced two practical commercial offerings that keep the core P2P app 100% free while funding ongoing relay infrastructure:

1. Firewall-Bypass TURN Relay Pro Pass (3 USDC / 3 Months)

For 90% of transfers, direct STUN works out of the box and is 100% free forever.

However, students behind university firewalls or colleagues in strict corporate networks with symmetric NATs cannot establish direct UDP hole-punches.

  • Pricing: 3 USDC for 3 months (just \$1/month).
  • Benefits:
    • Direct access to high-bandwidth TCP/TLS TURN relays over port 443 (which corporate firewalls cannot block).
    • Custom enterprise TURN server inputs: Users can plug in their own private coturn or Twilio TURN credentials directly into the client.
  • Client-Side Storage: The verified license and expiration timestamp are saved locally in localStorage, meaning zero accounts and zero tracked user data.

2. Custom White-Label Deployment for Teams & Agencies (30 USDC)

Video production agencies, law firms, and medical clinics frequently deal with sensitive multi-gigabyte files. They don't want their clients to see an AirStream logo, nor do they want to pay \$20–\$30/user/month to WeTransfer or Dropbox Teams.

For a one-time setup fee of 30 USDC:

  • Deployment on their custom domain (e.g. transfer.agency.com).
  • Custom branding, company logo, color palette, and favicon.
  • Dedicated private TURN relay with unthrottled bandwidth.
  • Full source code ownership & 24-hour turnaround.

What I Learned: Web3 as the Indie Hacker's Payment Rail

Building this convinced me that low-cost EVM networks like Base and Polygon are vastly underrated for indie web apps:

  1. Zero Merchant Approval: I didn't have to submit business registration forms, passports, or wait weeks for Stripe Atlas approval.
  2. Instant Global Reach: Anyone in the world with an internet connection can pay \$1 or \$30 without currency conversion penalties.
  3. No Database Burden: The blockchain serves as your payment database. You query receipts on-demand with open JSON-RPC endpoints.
  4. Keeps Open-Source Free: By charging for convenience (white-labeling) and infrastructure-heavy edge cases (TURN relays), the core P2P application stays 100% free, MIT-licensed, and community-driven.

Fuel the Dev (Tip Me a Coffee in USDC) ☕

Building and maintaining an open-source, privacy-first tool with zero tracking and zero cloud lock-in takes a lot of late nights and caffeine.

A tipping button shouldn't be masqueraded as a "product feature"—if AirStream genuinely saved your sanity, rescued you from a 2GB WeTransfer cap, or let you zap a 30GB video file across the room without paying a \$20/month SaaS subscription, feel free to fuel future development!

You can hit the Tip button directly on air-stream.pages.dev to send 1, 2, 5, or 10 USDC with 1-click via Rabby / MetaMask (gas on Base and Polygon is less than a penny!), or send directly to my EVM address:

Every micro-tip keeps the project independent, free from corporate ads, and 100% open-source for everyone.

articles.title: Show DEV: AirStream — Stream Gigabytes Browser-to-Browser with WebRTC (No Cloud, No Size Limits)
articles.description: Why upload an 8GB file to a cloud server just to download it again? Here's how I built AirStream: a browser-to-browser P2P file streamer and collaborative workspace.
articles.body_html:
TL;DR

🚀 Live Web App (Free, No Signup): air-stream.pages.dev

⭐ GitHub Repo (MIT): github.com/QuantumTechCoder/AirStream

🛠️ Stack: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS v4, WebRTC RTCDataChannel, Web Streams API, PeerJS WSS, Cloudflare Pages.

The Universal Modern Tragedy

Picture this: It's 2 AM. You just rendered a 6GB 4K video on your PC, and you need it on your phone or your teammate's MacBook across the room.

What are your options in 2026?

  1. WeTransfer: "Please upgrade to WeTransfer Pro to send files larger than 2GB." (And even if it fits, you have to wait 25 minutes for it to upload to an AWS S3 bucket in Virginia, only for the recipient to wait another 25 minutes to download it).
  2. Google Drive / Dropbox: "Your cloud storage is 99% full from vacation photos and PDF receipts from 2018."
  3. AirDrop: "Sorry, did we detect a Windows laptop or an Android phone? We don't do that here."
  4. The USB Flash Drive Dance: "Where is my USB-C to USB-A adapter? Why is this flash drive formatted in NTFS? Why won't Android mount it?!"

Why are we routing multi-gigabyte files through someone else's data center across the ocean when both devices are sitting on the exact same local Wi-Fi router?

So, as any reasonable developer with too much caffeine would do, I decided to build AirStream.

What is AirStream?

AirStream is a zero-install, Progressive Web App (PWA) that opens an encrypted, direct peer-to-peer data pipeline between any two browsers using WebRTC RTCDataChannel.

  • 🚫 Zero File Size Limits: Send 200MB, 5GB, or 50GB. The browser doesn't choke.
  • ⚡ The "Double Wait" is Dead: Bytes stream directly from Device A to Device B as they are being read. The recipient starts downloading the exact second you start sending.
  • 📶 Gigabit LAN Speeds: When both devices are on the same Wi-Fi or office network, transfers bypass your internet ISP completely, transferring at full router hardware speed (100MB/s+).
  • 🔒 End-to-End Encrypted: Data flows through DTLS-SRTP encrypted tunnels. No intermediate cloud server ever touches or stores your files.
  • 📱 Universal Cross-Platform: Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS Safari, Android Chrome—if it runs a modern browser, it works.
  • 📋 Collaborative Workspace: Because I was already in the WebRTC rabbit hole, I also baked in a Live Shared Clipboard and a Real-Time Collaborative Code Scratchpad (CodeMirror 6).

Under the Hood: The Deep Technical Challenges

Building a toy WebRTC chat app is easy. Building a system that reliably transfers 10GB+ binary files across hostile cellular firewalls without crashing the browser tab is a whole different beast.

Here are the biggest architectural hurdles I hit and how I solved them:

1. The "Tab Death" Out-Of-Memory Crash (Backpressure Control)

If you naively try to read a 5GB file using FileReader.readAsArrayBuffer() or shove slices into an RTCDataChannel in a while loop, you will instantly crash the user's browser tab.

Why? Because the browser's JavaScript engine will load the entire payload into RAM faster than the underlying OS socket can flush the packets over the network. The buffer explodes, memory spikes to multiple gigabytes, and the tab silently vanishes with an OutOfMemory error.

The Fix:
I implemented backpressure regulation using RTCDataChannel.bufferedAmount and bufferedAmountLowThreshold:

// Slicing files into 64KB framed binary chunks
const CHUNK_SIZE = 64 * 1024; // 64 KB

while (currentChunk < totalChunks && !isCancelled) {
  // If the internal WebRTC buffer exceeds 1MB, PAUSE the stream
  if (dataChannel.bufferedAmount > 1024 * 1024) {
    await new Promise<void>((resolve) => {
      dataChannel.bufferedAmountLowThreshold = 256 * 1024; // Wake up at 256KB
      dataChannel.onbufferedamountlow = () => {
        dataChannel.onbufferedamountlow = null;
        resolve();
      };
    });
  }

  // Safe to read next slice and transmit
  const slice = file.slice(start, end);
  const buffer = await slice.arrayBuffer();
  dataChannel.send(framePacket(currentChunk, fileId, buffer));
  currentChunk++;
}

By throttling chunk creation against the network driver's drain rate, RAM consumption stays flat under 50MB, regardless of whether you're streaming a 100MB video or a 50GB raw disk image.

2. The Packet Framing Protocol

WebRTC DataChannels don't inherently know where one file ends and another begins if you send raw buffers. To solve this, every 64KB slice is wrapped in a lightweight binary header:

[4 Bytes: Chunk Index (Uint32)]
[4 Bytes: File ID Length (Uint32)]
[N Bytes: File ID (UTF-8)]
[Remaining Bytes: Raw Binary Payload]

On the receiving end, the receiver parses the header, verifies chunk integrity, updates a moving-average transfer speed indicator (MB/s) and ETA countdown, and streams the chunks safely into an assembling Blob.

3. The "Cellular CGNAT" Nightmare (Wi-Fi ↔ Jio / Mobile Data)

During early testing, transfers worked flawlessly between two laptops on my home Wi-Fi. But the second I tested between my laptop (broadband) and my phone connected to 5G mobile data (Reliance Jio), it refused to connect.

Why? Mobile cellular carriers use aggressive Carrier-Grade NAT (CGNAT) with Symmetric NAT.

Standard public STUN servers (stun.l.google.com) only tell you your public IP and port. With Symmetric NAT, the firewall changes the external port mapping for every distinct destination. Direct UDP hole-punching is mathematically impossible between two symmetric NATs without a relay.

The Fix:

  1. Persistent WebSocket Signaling: We use a global persistent WebSocket signaling layer (0.peerjs.com) over port 443 WSS so offer/answer exchanges never drop across different ISP routing paths.
  2. Dual-Path STUN + Port 443 TURN Relay Fallback: We added OpenRelay TURN servers configured with TCP/TLS on port 443: 
export const ICE_SERVERS: RTCIceServer[] = [
  { urls: ['stun:stun.cloudflare.com:3478'] },
  { urls: ['stun:stun.l.google.com:19302'] },
  {
    urls: [
      'turn:openrelay.metered.ca:443?transport=tcp',
      'turns:openrelay.metered.ca:443?transport=tcp',
    ],
    username: 'openrelayproject',
    credential: 'openrelayproject',
  },
];

Because mobile networks never block port 443 (HTTPS), WebRTC seamlessly falls back to the relayed route whenever direct P2P is blocked by enterprise firewalls or carrier CGNATs.

4. The Collaborative Workspace (Clipboard & Code Editor)

Because WebRTC DataChannels allow multiplexed arbitrary data channels, AirStream also doubles as an instant device bridge for text, links, and code snippets:

Whether you need to quickly copy an authentication OTP, an API token, or write code together in real-time using CodeMirror 6 with full syntax highlighting (JS, TS, Python, Markdown, JSON), changes sync in sub-10 milliseconds.

5. The Air-Gapped / Offline QR Mode

What happens if you are in an airplane, a basement, or on a remote film set with an isolated local Wi-Fi router and zero internet access?

Because normal signaling requires an external server, AirStream includes a dedicated Offline / Air-Gapped SDP Exchanger:

Device A generates a base64-compressed SDP Offer as a QR code. Device B scans it with its camera, generates an Answer QR code, and Device A scans it back.

Boom. Direct peer-to-peer data transfer with zero connection to the outside internet.

Try It Out!

The project is live, MIT-licensed, and 100% free:

  1. Open air-stream.pages.dev on your laptop.
  2. Click Pair Devices and scan the QR code with your phone (or share the 6-character room code).
  3. Drop a file, paste into the live clipboard, or test the collaborative code scratchpad!

Let's Chat!

I'd love to hear your thoughts:

  • What's the weirdest or most cursed WebRTC edge case you've ever had to debug?
  • What file sizes or network setups should I stress-test next?
  • Would you find an auto-discovery feature (like mDNS / local LAN peer discovery) useful?

Drop your feedback below or star the repo on GitHub:

⭐ github.com/QuantumTechCoder/AirStream

articles.title: Is Coding with AI Actually Faster and Cheaper?
articles.description: How has AI actually changed the way we work? Are coding agents really making us remarkably faster?...
articles.body_html:
How has AI actually changed the way we work? Are coding agents really making us remarkably faster? And what if, instead of answering with “well, that's what I think,” we tried looking at some actual scientific research?

This is another article inspired by the upcoming AI Coding Summit in Berlin (and yes, I'll leave a link to my speaker badge at the end again, which I think might come with some discounts). I promised myself I wouldn't do this again, but, as usual, I've also signed up for three panel discussions. 😅 One of them has a title very similar to this article.

I wanted some hard data for that discussion, so I dug into the research. You'll find links to all the studies at the end.

And since today hasn't exactly been a great day for me, and I'd much rather be somewhere else, I figured I'd cheer myself up the usual way. By writing something for you!

Are we actually coding faster?

Let's start with the first question. Has AI really made us faster? If someone suddenly stopped me in the street and demanded an answer, I'd probably say yes. In my experience, we write code much faster now.

But that improvement doesn't seem to translate into an equally dramatic increase in how much software we actually deliver. After all, there's code review, analysis, discussions, and so on and so on. Sure, things are a bit faster. Maybe a little less stressful, too. But I wouldn't say the entire development process has suddenly become much quicker.

Then again, maybe it's just me? Maybe the rest of the world is already shipping features at the speed of light?

Well, apparently not.

A study by economists from MIT and Wharton, revised in September 2026, suggests that my intuition might not be entirely wrong. The researchers analyzed data from more than 500,000 GitHub developers and estimated the following cumulative changes associated with autonomous coding agents:

Metric Estimated change
Coding activity (commits) +240%
Software releases +30%
Total app usage across the marketplaces studied No overall increase

These are observational estimates. Still, the gap between the jump in commits and the increase in releases is pretty striking.

Okay, so we're committing a lot more and shipping somewhat more often. In my own work, it sometimes just feels a little less stressful. But it's hardly the revolution some people make it out to be. Maybe things look different in brand-new projects. In large, established systems like the ones I work on, I haven't seen anything close to a tenfold improvement.

Maybe that'll change when someone invents those super-self-healing-autonomous agents. For now, I sometimes feel like things are getting more complicated. With everything that's been happening around AI security lately, everyone seems to be getting a little obsessed with it. Myself very much included. 😅

But are individual developers actually faster?

Okay, we have more commits. But are we actually coding faster? Again, if I had to guess, I'd say yes, but not that much faster.

The data is mixed.

Study Result What was measured
Cui et al., Management Science, 2026 +26.08% Number of completed tasks
METR, July 2025 19% slower Time to complete tasks
Science, January 2026 +3.6% Estimated increase in quarterly coding activity on GitHub
Borg et al., June 2026 30.7% less time Median reduction in implementation time in the observational phase

Once again, the results are reasonably close to what I expected. I'm not going to spend the next ten paragraphs going over the methodology. If you're curious, the original studies are linked below. They looked at different developers, tools, and tasks, and each percentage measures something different.

Several of these studies do point to gains, though. We're not all suddenly 10x developers. xD But there are real improvements.

METR is the odd one out here. It's from 2025, which, in the current AI world, practically makes it ancient history. But I love one detail about it.

Before the experiment, developers expected AI to make them about 24% faster. The actual result? They were 19% slower! And even after the experiment, they still thought AI had made them faster.

It shows how much we can fool ourselves until we actually measure things. I swear, this applies to practically every area of life. For example, I used to think I barely ate anything. 😂

To be fair, METR published an update in February 2026. The researchers think newer tools are likely to be more helpful, but their follow-up couldn't reliably estimate the speedup because of who was willing to participate.

Okay, but is software development actually cheaper?

If someone woke me up at midnight and asked whether AI had made software development cheaper, I'd probably say no. At least not yet.

The 2025 DORA research and a follow-up published in March 2026 point to something many of us have written about. Some of the time we save writing code goes straight into auditing and verifying it. So the savings on implementation can shrink by the time the change gets to production. DORA describes where that work can shift, leaving the overall cost question open.

Yes, yes, I've heard about multi-agent teams where one agent writes the code, another reviews it, another tests it, and then it all goes into production. I'm sure that can work in some situations. I'd be very cautious about trying that trick in a mission-critical system. Financial software, for example. Good luck with that strategy 😂🤞

What about the cost of tokens?

One last question. Are we spending all the money we save by writing code faster on tokens?

I have to admit, the answer surprised me! If I had to guess, I'd have said yes, especially if you blindly use the most expensive models for absolutely everything.

But the findings are more interesting than that! Two recent studies looked at the economics of AI-assisted software development. One was published in September 2026 by Potluri and colleagues, and the other in October 2026 by Steffen Herbold.

Both suggest that the effectiveness of an AI agent can matter more than the price of the tokens it consumes. In Potluri's analysis, models that solved more tasks produced substantial estimated savings, while less effective models ended up costing more in many task categories. A cheap model can get expensive pretty quickly if it keeps failing and you have to pay for another try.

Herbold simulated 432 scenarios for teams using a mix of developers and AI agents. He included salaries, token costs, supervision, bugs, and technical debt. Teams with highly capable agents were usually cheaper than teams of developers working without AI. The results for less capable agents were mixed. In the simulation, agent capability mattered more than token price because better results cut the cost of checking and fixing the work.

Herbold's results come from simulations, and Potluri's estimates come from benchmarks and economic modeling. So we have two ways of estimating when the savings might outweigh the token bill. The actual cost of building and maintaining commercial software is a much bigger question.

So, what's the verdict?

It looks like AI really can make coding faster and cheaper. Several studies show gains on specific tasks, and the economic models suggest that capable agents can save money even after you pay for the tokens.

We still have less evidence about whether the total cost of building, delivering, securing, and maintaining software has fallen across the industry.

So far, the research mostly lines up with what a lot of us seem to feel. Skynet may already be sharpening its weapons, but it hasn't conquered the world just yet. 😅

And what about you? Do these findings reflect your experience? Has AI genuinely made your team faster and cheaper, or does it look completely different where you work?

I'd love to hear your thoughts!

If you enjoyed this article, you can also follow me on LinkedIn.

And if you'd like access to free materials from AI Coding Summit, you can register using my speaker badge.

https://metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/

https://doi.org/10.1007/s10664-026-10889-1
https://dora.dev/research/2025/dora-report/
https://dora.dev/insights/balancing-ai-tensions/

articles.title: Why I Rewrote type-tune from TypeScript to Rust 🦀
articles.description: Hoi hoi! 👋  I'm @nyaomaru, a frontend engineer who loves TypeScript and gambas, not crabs! 🦐  And...
articles.body_html:
Hoi hoi! 👋

I'm @nyaomaru, a frontend engineer who loves TypeScript and gambas, not crabs! 🦐

And yet, somehow, I ended up building a tool in Rust. 🙀🦀

Recently, I released a new open-source CLI tool called type-tune.

necoz-oss / type-tune

A Rust-powered CLI to find shared TypeScript types and move them safely. 🦀

type-tune

Give shared TypeScript types a better home. 😸

Scan. Review. Move. Validate.

type-tune is a Rust-powered CLI that finds shared TypeScript type aliases and interface declarations and helps move them without manually chasing imports.

It creates a reviewable plan, updates supported type imports and re-exports, and validates the rewrite with TypeScript. You decide what moves and where.

Guides for installation, the first scan, and the review workflow live in the official documentation. Releases are listed on GitHub Releases, and the package is type-tune on npm.

Why type-tune?

Types often start next to a component or utility, then end up shared across a project. Moving them later means tracking imports, local dependencies, and barrels by hand.

  • Discover shared types with deterministic candidate IDs.
  • Review plan.md and choose the destination before making changes.
  • Rewrite supported type-only imports, aliases, and simple barrels while keeping compatibility re-exports at the original…
View on GitHub

type-tune finds shared TypeScript types and helps move them to a better place without manually updating imports, dependencies, and barrel exports.

But why is a TypeScript tool created by a TypeScript lover written in Rust? 🤔

🐈 It All Started with TypeScript

Naturally, the original implementation of type-tune was written in TypeScript.

It was already complete by September, with nearly 20,000 lines of TypeScript, including tests, comments, and blank lines.

Around that time, I happened to watch this video by DHH.

I didn't agree with everything, but I particularly liked the idea of taking advantage of this era to pursue things that genuinely excite us.

Of course, outside of personal projects, I don't think we can simply hand everything over to AI. Someone still needs to understand and maintain the software.

But while watching the video, a simple thought crossed my mind.

If it's possible to go from Rails to Rust, why not TypeScript to Rust? 🦀

🦀 From TypeScript to Rust

I already had a working implementation, design documents, tests, and well-defined TypeScript types.

For example, translating a data model like this:

type CandidateKind = "typeAlias" | "interface";

type Candidate = {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  kind: CandidateKind;
  referrers: string[];
};

Into something like this:

enum CandidateKind {
    TypeAlias,
    Interface,
}

struct Candidate {
    id: String,
    name: String,
    kind: CandidateKind,
    referrers: Vec<String>,
}

Of course, migrating the entire application involved much more than translating type definitions.

But having an existing design and implementation made it much easier.

With the help of AI, I completed the migration in less than a month while working on it as a side project.

The results were satisfying 😻

  • Better execution performance.
  • Native binary distribution.
  • No Rust development environment required for npm users.

You can still install type-tune like any other familiar TypeScript development tool.

pnpm add -D type-tune

The npm launcher requires Node.js 22+, but the core implementation runs as a native binary.

So far, so good!

Except for one little problem. 😿

🙀 type-tune Got Faster. Its Developer Got Slower.

I barely knew Rust. 😹

I'm comfortable reviewing AI-generated TypeScript code, but with Rust, I'm still learning the fundamentals.

For example, consider ownership and borrowing.

In TypeScript, this is perfectly fine:

function printName(name: string) {
  console.log(name);
}

const name = "OrderSummary";

printName(name);
console.log(name); // OK

However, a similar implementation in Rust doesn't compile.

fn print_name(name: String) {
    println!("{}", name);
}

fn main() {
    let name = String::from("OrderSummary");

    print_name(name);
    println!("{}", name); // Error: value borrowed after move
}

The ownership of name is transferred to print_name.

One way to fix this is to borrow the value instead.

fn print_name(name: &str) {
    println!("{}", name);
}

fn main() {
    let name = String::from("OrderSummary");

    print_name(&name);
    println!("{}", name); // OK
}

Another option is to clone the value.

print_name(name.clone());
println!("{}", name); // OK

Both solutions compile, but cloning unnecessarily can introduce additional allocations.

So when AI generates a .clone(), I need to understand whether it's actually necessary or whether borrowing would be more appropriate.

The same applies to visibility boundaries.

For example, making an internal helper public might solve an accessibility issue:

pub fn resolve_destination() {
    // ...
}

But if the function is only used within the same crate, exposing it publicly may be unnecessary.

pub(crate) fn resolve_destination() {
    // ...
}

And if it's only used within its own module, it can remain private.

fn resolve_destination() {
    // ...
}

The compiler accepts all three declarations, but each represents a different architectural decision.

I'm also still learning when macros are appropriate and when ordinary functions are sufficient.

AI can generate code that compiles, but I still need to understand whether its design choices are appropriate.

In TypeScript, I can make these decisions relatively quickly. In Rust, I often need to stop and learn something before continuing my review.

AI can generate Rust code much faster than I can understand it.

I wanted to accelerate the development of my side project, but I introduced a new bottleneck.

Myself.

What a wonderful optimization! 😹

🎨 Creating Without Learning

Of course, I could just vibe code.

I could keep pressing Enter whenever AI asks for approval and probably release features faster.

But for me, creating something without learning anything is just another task.

And I believe that if I keep doing nothing but those tasks, I'll gradually lose my ability to create.

I enjoy using AI to learn unfamiliar concepts and explore new approaches.

But I don't want to spend my time simply producing things without understanding them.

I don't want to become a very expensive Enter key. 😹

Do I regret choosing Rust?

Not at all!

It was a valuable experience, and I'm grateful that we live in a time when we can challenge ourselves like this so easily.

Now, let's talk about what I actually built!

🛠️ The Design Behind type-tune

One architectural decision remained unchanged throughout the migration.

Scan / Plan / Apply

Consider a typical TypeScript project.

src/
├── features/
│   ├── orders/
│   │   └── order-page.ts
│   ├── dashboard/
│   │   └── dashboard.ts
│   └── reports/
│       └── reports.ts

Initially, a type belongs to the orders feature.

// features/orders/order-page.ts

export type OrderSummary = {
  id: string;
  total: number;
};

But as the application grows, other features start importing it.

// features/dashboard/dashboard.ts

import type { OrderSummary } from "../orders/order-page";

export function calculateRevenue(orders: OrderSummary[]) {
  return orders.reduce((sum, order) => sum + order.total, 0);
}

// features/reports/reports.ts

import type { OrderSummary } from "../orders/order-page";

export function createReport(order: OrderSummary) {
  return `${order.id}: ${order.total}`;
}

The type is still useful, but its original location may no longer be appropriate.

Tools like Knip help us remove unused code.

type-tune tackles a different problem: reorganizing types that are still in use.

🔍 1. Scan 

pnpm exec type-tune scan --project tsconfig.json

type-tune analyzes exported type aliases, interfaces, references, and relevant dependencies to identify potential extraction candidates.

No source code is modified.

📋 2. Plan

Finding a type that can be moved doesn't necessarily mean it should be moved.

That's why type-tune generates a reviewable plan.

pnpm exec type-tune plan \
  --project tsconfig.json \
  --out .type-tune/plan.json \
  --markdown .type-tune/plan.md

It generates two files:

  • plan.json — Candidate metadata and validation information.
  • plan.md — A human-readable, editable plan.

Every candidate is ignored by default.

Here's a simplified example of plan.md:

- [ignore] <candidate-id> `OrderSummary`
  - kind: `typeAlias`
  - from: `src/features/orders/order-page.ts`
  - to: `src/features/orders/types/order.ts`

You can approve the candidate and customize its destination.

- [ignore] <candidate-id> OrderSummary
+ [apply] <candidate-id> OrderSummary
    - kind: typeAlias
    - from: src/features/orders/order-page.ts
-   - to: src/features/orders/types/order.ts
+   - to: src/domains/orders/types/order-summary.ts

Perhaps it belongs in a shared directory, a domain-specific module, or exactly where it is now.

That's an architectural decision.

You decide what moves and where.

🚚 3. Apply

Preview the selected changes:

pnpm exec type-tune apply \
  --plan .type-tune/plan.json \
  --markdown .type-tune/plan.md \
  --dry-run

Then apply them:

pnpm exec type-tune apply \
  --plan .type-tune/plan.json \
  --markdown .type-tune/plan.md

The resulting project structure:

src/
├── domains/
│   └── orders/
│       └── types/
│           └── order-summary.ts  ← Moved!
└── features/
    ├── orders/
    │   └── order-page.ts
    ├── dashboard/
    │   └── dashboard.ts
    └── reports/
        └── reports.ts

The type now lives in its new home.

// domains/orders/types/order-summary.ts

export type OrderSummary = {
  id: string;
  total: number;
};

Supported imports are updated automatically.

- import type { OrderSummary } from "../orders/order-page";
+ import type { OrderSummary } from "../../domains/orders/types/order-summary";

And the original module retains a compatibility re-export.

// features/orders/order-page.ts

export type { OrderSummary } from "../../domains/orders/types/order-summary";

type-tune also validates the rewrite using the TypeScript compiler and rolls back changes if normal validation fails.

You should still review the resulting diff and run your project-specific tests and builds.

🧩 Automate the Work, Not the Decisions

Why separate Scan, Plan, and Apply?

Because discovering opportunities, making architectural decisions, and executing changes are different responsibilities.

type-tune even supports optional AI-assisted review:

pnpm exec type-tune plan \
  --project tsconfig.json \
  --ai-review \
  --ai-dry-run

AI can provide additional review notes, but it doesn't control the source code rewrite. The command above previews the AI review request without contacting a provider.

Interestingly, this is also how I want to work with AI in my own development.

Automate the tedious work without taking architectural decisions away from developers.

That's the philosophy behind type-tune.

💚 Give Your TypeScript Types a Better Home!

You can start by simply scanning your project.

npx type-tune scan --project tsconfig.json

No need to move anything yet. Just see what you find! 😸

necoz-oss / type-tune

A Rust-powered CLI to find shared TypeScript types and move them safely. 🦀

type-tune

Give shared TypeScript types a better home. 😸

Scan. Review. Move. Validate.

type-tune is a Rust-powered CLI that finds shared TypeScript type aliases and interface declarations and helps move them without manually chasing imports.

It creates a reviewable plan, updates supported type imports and re-exports, and validates the rewrite with TypeScript. You decide what moves and where.

Guides for installation, the first scan, and the review workflow live in the official documentation. Releases are listed on GitHub Releases, and the package is type-tune on npm.

Why type-tune?

Types often start next to a component or utility, then end up shared across a project. Moving them later means tracking imports, local dependencies, and barrels by hand.

  • Discover shared types with deterministic candidate IDs.
  • Review plan.md and choose the destination before making changes.
  • Rewrite supported type-only imports, aliases, and simple barrels while keeping compatibility re-exports at the original…


View on GitHub


type-tune-docs.vercel.app

Feedback, ideas, issues, and contributions are always welcome!

And if you're a Rust developer, please teach this poor TypeScript cat how to become a competent crab. 😹🦀

Small. Simple. Useful. Built Together!

Thank you for reading! 🙌💚
