articles.body_html:
This is Part 6 of a series building an HL7 v2-to-FHIR R4 interoperability service in public. The repository is ND-codes/nhs-interop-platform,
and the code as it stood for this article is tagged part-6.

This week's plan was a ten-minute tour of the repository and the questions an interviewer asks about it. Before writing the tour, I did the obvious thing and followed the one I already had.

It doesn't work on a machine that isn't mine. Not in a subtle way.

A walkthrough is a promise

Most of what a repository claims is hard to check. A threat model, an
architecture diagram, a note about scaling: a reader takes those on trust or not at all.

A quickstart is different. It is a sequence of commands with stated outcomes, and the reader finds out within minutes whether you were telling the truth. It is the most falsifiable document in the repository and usually the least tested, because the author is the one person who can never run it fresh.

Mine had four failures. Three of them break on the reader's machine and work perfectly on mine. The fourth was not about machines at all.

make test could not run outside Git Bash

Step 7 of my quickstart said make test. The recipe:

docker run --rm -v "$$(cygpath -m $$(cd services/$$svc && pwd))":/app -w //app python:3.12-slim \
  sh -c "pip install -q -r requirements-dev.txt && pytest -q"

cygpath converts a Windows path into the C:/ form Docker wants. It exists
in Git Bash on Windows and nowhere else. On macOS or Linux that line is
cygpath: command not found, and make test and make lint both die on the
first service.

I work in Git Bash on Windows. It had never once failed for me, which is the entire problem.

The fix keeps the Windows behaviour exactly and adds the other path:

abs=$(cd services/$svc && pwd) ; wd=/app ;
if command -v cygpath >/dev/null 2>&1 ; then abs=$(cygpath -m "$abs") ; wd=//app ; fi ;
docker run --rm -v "$abs":/app -w "$wd" python:3.12-slim ...

The doubled //app is the other half of the same problem. MSYS rewrites a leading /app into a Windows path, so Git Bash needs it doubled and nothing else does. Both branches were tested, the second by putting a fake cygpath on PATH. Then the Git Bash branch ran for real on my machine: 92 tests, all
passing.

make integration installed into the system interpreter 

python3 -m pip install --quiet httpx pytest

On Debian, Ubuntu and Homebrew Python 3.11 and later, that is refused outright. PEP 668 lets a distribution mark its base interpreter as externally managed, and pip then declines with error: externally-managed-environment. It works on my machine because my Python is not marked that way.

It builds a throwaway virtualenv now, with a bin and Scripts fallback so the same line works in Git Bash.

A file the quickstart told you to copy did not exist 

cp terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars

There was no terraform.tfvars.example. There never had been. You only find that by following your own instructions as though you had not written them.

The alert that reached nobody

The fourth is the one worth the article, and I did not find it. Nan, a reader of Part 4, did.

Part 4 was about an alert that could never fire, because it watched a metric no service exported. I fixed that, exported the gauge, wrote the rule unit tests, added the runbook sections, and built scripts to open the circuit breaker on purpose so you could watch PDSCircuitOpen go Firing.

Nan's question was roughly: and then who gets told?

Nobody. Here is the whole chain:

  • observability/alertmanager/alertmanager.yml exists, and is a reasonable config. It routes by severity, groups by alertname and service, and has an inhibit rule.
  • Nothing starts an Alertmanager. There is no such service in Docker Compose and no such manifest anywhere in k8s/.
  • prometheus.yml had no alerting block, so even if one had been running, Prometheus did not know where it was.
  • That config's smtp_smarthost pointed at mailhog:1025. No file in the repository has ever started a mailhog.

So the rules evaluated, turned red in the Prometheus UI, and stopped there.
Meanwhile docs/architecture.md said "Alertmanager routes pages" and the runbook's prerequisites told the on-call engineer they would need access to "the alerts Slack/PagerDuty queue".

Part 4 made the alert fireable. Part 5 made the documentation honest about the controls. Neither of us noticed that the last hop did not exist, and it is the hop that makes the other two matter. An alert nobody receives is a dashboard.

The fix is small, which is the irritating part:

alerting:
  alertmanagers:
    - static_configs:
        - targets: ['alertmanager:9093']

Plus two services in Compose. Alertmanager and Mailpit as the destination: a disposable SMTP sink with a web inbox, which holds mail in memory and forwards it nowhere. That is what makes it safe to point a demo at. I used Mailpit rather than the MailHog the old config named, because MailHog has not been released since 2020 and Part 5 was about not shipping things you would not defend.

Now make break-pds opens the breaker, PDSCircuitOpen goes Firing about two minutes later, and the notification arrives at a web inbox on port 8025 where you can read it. The whole path, end to end, is a demo you can run on a laptop.

I ran it on 17 November, and again this morning for the screenshots. The subject line began [FIRING:1] PDSCircuitOpen transform. Six parts in, it is the first alert this project has ever delivered to anything.

The inbox also holds two IngestNoTraffic alerts I did not ask for. I checked the rule in alerts.yml before calling it a fault: it fires once ingest has gone 15 minutes without an HL7 message, and the stack sat idle overnight. So it is expected, but a demo stack left running will email you about its own quiet.

Making the tour testable

The underlying failure is that a quickstart is prose, and prose does not run in CI. So the tour is now a script, and make walkthrough runs it.

Eight checks. The stack is up, ingest accepts an ADT, the Patient reaches FHIR keyed on the NHS number, a lab result produces Observations, Prometheus is scraping every service, Prometheus has discovered an Alertmanager, Alertmanager is healthy, and the inbox is reachable. Each one fails loudly and stops.

The sixth is the one that would have caught Nan's finding:

discovered=$(curl -sf "$PROM/api/v1/alertmanagers" \
  | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(len(json.load(sys.stdin)["data"]["activeAlertmanagers"]))')
[ "$discovered" -ge 1 ] || fail "Prometheus has no active Alertmanager."

Two small things I would do again. The FHIR checks parse the Bundle rather than grepping for "total", because the whitespace is not guaranteed and a grep for that string also matches a zero. And the Mailpit check asserts reachability but reads the message count defensively, because I could not get Mailpit's API documentation to load and I was not willing to assert a field name I had not seen. A schema change should not turn a working inbox into a failed tour.

The tour failed its own first run

The script was written and checked without a Docker daemon. The first time it ran against a real stack, it stopped at check 3:

[3/8] The Patient reaches FHIR, keyed on the NHS number
      FAIL the Patient did not become true within 30s

The Patient was there. Asking HAPI for a count returned one. The query was the problem. A FHIR token search separates system and code with a pipe,
identifier=https://fhir.nhs.uk/Id/nhs-number|9000000009, and RFC 3986 does
not allow an unencoded | in a query string. HAPI runs on Tomcat, which enforces that by default and answers HTTP 400.

The 400 never reached the screen. curl -sf turns any HTTP error into a silent non-zero exit, and the retry loop read that as "not there yet". Thirty seconds later it reported a missing Patient that was never missing.

The fix is %7C in place of the pipe, in the script and in the quickstart. The quickstart needed it too: Tomcat's own documentation says the major browsers send that character unencoded, so the link would have failed in a browser as well.

This is the alert story again, at a smaller scale. A check that cannot tell "not found" from "you asked the wrong way" will pass or fail for the wrong reason, and you only find out by running it.

Four things the architecture document still claimed

While I was at it. docs/architecture.md said messages are dead-lettered to S3, which Part 5 established is false. It said GitLab CI gates quality, two weeks after we deleted .gitlab-ci.yml. It said CI pushes to an image registry, which it does not, because there is nowhere to push to. And it said "every request is traced", when what actually exists is a trace id carried in log lines. That is correlation, not distributed tracing, and there is no OpenTelemetry in any of these services.

All four are corrected in place, with a short note saying what each one used to claim. Quietly editing them would have been tidier and worse.

The questions an interviewer actually asks

This is the other half of what Part 6 was meant to cover, and the walkthrough work made it easier rather than harder, because the questions people ask about a system are mostly the ones a broken walkthrough exposes.

Walk me through what happens to a message.

It arrives at POST /hl7 on ingest, which validates the MSH segment and assigns a trace id. Transform parses it, maps it to a FHIR R4 transaction Bundle, optionally enriches the Patient from PDS, and writes the Bundle to HAPI FHIR with a conditional update keyed on the NHS number. Failures dead-letter to a local path. The trace id
follows the message through all three services.

What happens when PDS is down?

Enrichment fails open. A circuit breaker
opens after five consecutive failures, and the pipeline keeps writing Patients with locally derived demographics. Data quality degrades; no clinical message is dropped. That is a deliberate trade-off and it is the seventh Caldicott principle in practice, the one that says the duty to share can matter as much as the duty to protect. You can watch it with make break-pds.

Who gets paged?

Until this week, nobody, and I would say exactly that. The
rules evaluated and notified no one. It is fixed for the local stack and still missing in Kubernetes. A question like this is a gift, because the honest answer is more interesting than the tidy one.

How do you know the mapping is correct?

Unit tests per defect, each written to fail against the previous code. Part 3 covers nine specific ways an HL7 v2 to FHIR mapping goes wrong, most of them found by readers. The honest limit is that there is no conformance suite and no validation against the HL7 v2 to FHIR
implementation guide; the tests encode the defects we know about.

Where does patient data live and for how long?

Mapped fields in HAPI FHIR on Postgres. Complete raw messages in the dead-letter path, which holds more patient data than the FHIR store does, for up to 72 hours. That retention is new as of Part 5 and the path still does not survive a pod restart.

What is the worst bug you have shipped here?

Part 4's fix for the alert that could never fire. The circuit breaker was applied as a decorator to a coroutine function, so it counted the returned coroutine object as a success and never opened, which means the gauge I had just added and the alert I had just made fireable still could not fire. The test passed because it drove the breaker synchronously. I found it by running the stack.

How would you scale it?

The ingest-to-transform hop is synchronous HTTP,
which keeps the local demo one command and is the first thing I would replace with an SQS FIFO queue using the NHS number as the message group id so a patient's messages stay ordered. Beyond that the services are stateless and scale horizontally; the bottleneck is the FHIR write path.

What would you do differently?

Wrote the documentation last. Almost every false claim in this repository was true of the design at the moment it was
written and never revisited.

What I did not fix

There is still no Alertmanager in the Helm charts, so the Kubernetes path notifies nobody. I did not write one, because I cannot deploy a cluster to test it and shipping untested YAML two days before publishing is the exact thing Part 5 was about. It is in the "Claimed, not built" section of docs/security.md and a roadmap issue.

There is no paging integration anywhere. The Alertmanager config has a PagerDuty receiver commented out and has never been pointed at a routing key.

make restore-pds brings PDS back but does not clear the alert. The breaker only tries the call again when the next request arrives, so with no traffic it stays open and PDSCircuitOpen keeps firing after the outage is over. One synthetic message closed it. The restore script should send that message, and the runbook should say so. That is next week's pull request.

The retry loop still hides the status code. The pipe is fixed, but the next malformed query would fail the same silent way.

And I have not timed the tour on a second machine. The series plan called this part a ten-minute walkthrough; the document now says the figure should be yours rather than mine.

Worth stealing

Run your own quickstart on a machine you did not configure. A colleague's, a fresh VM, a container. The author is the one person who cannot test it.

Grep your build tooling for anything platform-specific. cygpath, open, sed -i with a bare -i, realpath, date -d. Each one quietly scopes your repository to one operating system.

Make the tour a target. Prose cannot run in CI; a script can, and then the document and the repository cannot drift apart silently.

Check the last hop of anything that is supposed to tell a human. Working alert rules that notify nobody look identical to working alerting from inside the repository.

Correct a stale claim in place, with a line saying what it used to say. The
edit history is not where a reader looks.

Where AI helps here, and where it doesn't

I built this with Claude Code, and this week drew the line unusually clearly.

Reading the Makefile and noticing that cygpath is Git Bash only is exactly the kind of thing it is good at. So is knowing that PEP 668 would refuse the pip line, and checking terraform.tfvars.example against the variables that are actually declared. That sweep took minutes, and I would not have done it by hand two days before publishing.

But none of that is the same as running the thing. It wrote and checked this week's changes in a sandbox with no Docker daemon, so "works on my machine" problems were invisible to it by construction. It found the cygpath problem by reading, after I pointed it at the walkthrough, which is not the same as the problem announcing itself.

The walkthrough script is the clearest example. It was reviewed, shellchecked and clean, and it failed its first real run on a URL encoding rule. Once the stack was up on my machine, the same assistant ran the query directly, found the 400 in about a minute, and checked the fix against the RFC and Tomcat's documentation. Reading wrote the bug. Running found it.

The alert delivery gap is the sharper case. It was not found by reading at all, by a model or by me. Nan found it by asking the one question neither of us had: and then who gets told? Two articles in a row went past it while looking directly at the alerting configuration.

The pattern I would now state plainly, three weeks running: reading finds inconsistencies, running finds defects, and other people find the questions.

Sources

  • PEP 668, on externally managed Python environments
  • Prometheus configuration, for the top-level alerting block
  • Prometheus HTTP API, for the /api/v1/alertmanagers response shape
  • RFC 3986, section 3.4, the characters allowed in a URI query
  • Apache Tomcat HTTP connector, relaxedQueryChars and the characters rejected by default
  • Mailpit, Docker install
  • The Caldicott Principles, National Data Guardian
  • Alertmanager and Prometheus configurations in this article were validated with amtool check-config 0.34.1 and promtool check config

Next

Part 7 is the last one: where AI fits in this work and where it does not, with seven weeks of specifics rather than opinions.

If you have a quickstart in a repository you maintain, run it somewhere else this week. What broke first?

This is a personal project. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by NHS England or any NHS organisation. It uses the public PDS FHIR sandbox and synthetic test data only. Views are my own.

Hey Folks 👋

As software engineers and programmers these days have transitioned to a more AI driven workflow, if we are not building for AI then at least we are using it to some extent in our day-to-day lives, from answering questions, writing the syntax, and even pushing code for you while you are asleep.

My own issues and problems these days

I have had issues with my teeth since I was a kid, growing up I didn't like going to the dentist and thus here I'm at 22 with a bunch of dental issues. Thankfully I decided to fix all of my dental issues and underdoing in one go the past summer, which I did and I'm proudly happy about it, except for my improperly aligned teeth, so I decided to put on clear aligners to help solve that problem once and for all, which would mean all of my dentist-related issues would be gone at once.

You might be asking how does that even relate to AI and what's the relation. Well, I will answer you now.

Programmers and engineers like to see problems and then build solutions for them, and in my day 2 of wearing the aligners, I had realized that I don't know how long I'm taking them off every day, because these aligners have strict 21+ hours per day requirement, and to me that sounds like an SLA that must be met.

It was amazing that in 30 minutes and a single prompt, Claude managed to whip up a native Swift UI app for me that I can have installed on my phone which I carry with me almost every minute of the day, hook it up with Apple ShortCuts and Siri, so I can track exactly how many hours I'm putting them in, and how much time I take them off, track my average daily wearing time, and send me reminders for its the day for me to put on the next aligner so I can easily track my treatment plan from the device I have access to at almost all times.

Now would I sell or even publish such an app? Absolutely not!
But I find it fascinating how identifying problems, then detailing them to models like Claude or Codex and seeing how amazing of a result you would get in such a brink of time, given that if I had to do that myself, it would've probably taken me the months of the treatment plan period which is 7 months to build an app with such UI, a theme, and all the features it managed to pack into it.

Here are some screenshots from the app

It is incredible that now we a few minutes you can build what would have taken days, and it's also incredible that you no longer have what's so niche and that you would have to wait until someone builds the thing that solves your own problem. You could have an absolutely one-off case and still can get an app or a website or any sort of interface that will satisfy your own needs.

Have you found yourself in such a situation yet?

I have been using AI to ship code to production for months now, but never had the need for such an app to solve a given problem that I had just began facing in my life, which led me to have an agent build me such an app, but what about you? Have you had any of these experiences yet? What was the problem you had solved for yourself with these tools?

articles.title: Twelve Files for Twenty Lines: When Clean Code Becomes the Problem
articles.description: I've seen perfectly clean code that nobody could change. Over-engineering dresses up as good practice. Here's how I tell the difference, what it costs in cognitive load, and the ugly function I now defend in review.
articles.body_html:
I've seen code that ticked every box. Small functions. One responsibility per class. Interfaces everywhere. Not a single line you could call ugly.

And nobody could change it.

I remember one ticket: add an optional phone number to a form. We estimated half a day. It took three, and twelve files. Most of that time didn't go into changing the code. It went into finding where things happened.

To understand what happened when a user clicked "Save", you had to follow six jumps: a handler that called a service that called a factory that built a strategy that delegated to a mapper that finally touched the data. Twenty lines of real logic, spread thin over an architecture built for a future that never came.

Everyone who had written it was proud of it. Everyone who had to maintain it was afraid of it. Not because any piece was hard. Because you had to hold all of them in your head at once.

We don't talk about this enough. We have a hundred articles on how to clean up messy code. We have very few on the opposite failure, because the opposite failure looks like virtue.

What it looks like

Here's an illustration. Not real code from a real project, but if you've been around, you've met its cousins.

The task: apply a discount to an order if the customer is a member.

// DiscountStrategy.ts
export interface DiscountStrategy {
  apply(amount: number): number
}

// MemberDiscountStrategy.ts
export class MemberDiscountStrategy implements DiscountStrategy {
  apply(amount: number) { return amount * 0.9 }
}

// NoDiscountStrategy.ts
export class NoDiscountStrategy implements DiscountStrategy {
  apply(amount: number) { return amount }
}

// DiscountStrategyFactory.ts
export class DiscountStrategyFactory {
  create(customer: Customer): DiscountStrategy {
    return customer.isMember
      ? new MemberDiscountStrategy()
      : new NoDiscountStrategy()
  }
}

// OrderPricingService.ts
export class OrderPricingService {
  constructor(private factory: DiscountStrategyFactory) {}
  price(order: Order) {
    return this.factory.create(order.customer).apply(order.amount)
  }
}

Five files. Every one of them is "clean". Each class has one job, each name is honest, each piece is testable alone.

And here's the same thing:

function priceOf(order: Order) {
  const discount = order.customer.isMember ? 0.9 : 1
  return order.amount * discount
}

Three lines. You read it once and you know everything.

"But what if we add more discount types?" Then you'll change it, on the day you add them, knowing what they actually look like. Which is almost never what you imagined a year before.

The cost nobody measures

Count the files and you still miss the real price. The real price is paid in your head.

To read the three-line version, you hold one thing in mind. To read the five-file version, you hold five: the interface, the two strategies, the factory, the service, and how they connect. None of them is hard. But you have to keep all of them loaded at once to answer one question: what does a member pay?

That's cognitive load, and to me it's the main problem with this kind of code. Working memory is small. Every jump spends some of it on the structure instead of on the problem. By the sixth jump, you've forgotten why you opened the first file.

No linter reports it. No coverage tool measures it. It shows up elsewhere: in onboarding that takes months, in estimates that double, in the bug nobody wants to pick up.

"AI will handle it"

I hear this more and more. The model writes the twelve files in seconds, and it can walk you through them too. So who cares about the indirection?

I do. Typing was never the bottleneck. Understanding is. AI makes structure cheap to produce, which makes it cheap to produce more structure than anyone can hold in their head.

This part is personal opinion: the day you lose your grip on your own code, you lose the core of the job. My test is simple. When someone tells me "it's broken here", I want to know right away which file to open, where to put the breakpoint, what to test. If I need a tool to explain my own codebase before I can start debugging, it isn't really my code anymore.

Why we do it

I've been that developer. I think most of us have, right after we discovered design patterns.

The first reason is that rules are easier than judgment. "Functions should be short" can be checked by a linter. "This code should be easy to change" can't. So we optimize what we can measure, and a codebase can score perfectly on every rule and still be miserable to work in.

The second is fear. An abstraction "just in case" feels like insurance. It isn't. Insurance pays when the accident happens. A speculative abstraction costs you every day, and when the real requirement arrives, it's usually the wrong shape, and now you have to undo it first.

The third is harder to admit. Elegant code is satisfying to write. That's not a crime. But the reader doesn't get the pleasure. They only get the indirection.

How I tell the difference now

Clean code isn't the code that ticks the most rules. It's the code the next developer understands quickly and changes without fear.

So I've replaced the rules with four questions:

  1. How many files do I open to change one behavior? If the answer is more than two or three for a small change, the structure is working against me.
  2. Can I point to the second use? An interface with one implementation is a question, not an answer. I want to see the second caller before I build for it.
  3. Could a newcomer follow it in one sitting? If understanding a click takes six jumps, the code isn't clean. It's hidden.
  4. When it breaks, do I know which file to open? If a bug report doesn't point me somewhere within seconds, I've lost the map of my own code.

And a habit that follows from them: sometimes I defend the ugly function. Thirty lines, top to bottom, a few ifs, readable at a glance. In review, someone suggests splitting it into five. I ask what we gain, and who it's for.

Sometimes the answer is good, and we split it. Often there isn't one.

What finally got that codebase simplified wasn't a refactoring plan. A new developer joined, spent two weeks on a one-line fix, and asked in a retro why saving a form needed six classes. Nobody in the room had a good answer. So we started inlining, one flow at a time, each time we had to touch one.

What I'm not saying

I'm not saying patterns are bad, or that a 400-line function is fine. I wrote a whole article about the principles I code by, and I stand by them. KISS and YAGNI are on that list for a reason: they're the two principles that protect you from the others.

The goal was never beauty. It's maintainability. Most of the time they agree. When they don't, I know which one I'm paid for.

Have you ever worked in code that was too clean to maintain? What did it look like, and what finally got it simplified? And does AI change the answer for you?

I write about front-end architecture and modernizing legacy code. More on my site. Let's talk on LinkedIn.

articles.title: CrossRoads: A Mirror, Not a Verdict - Exploring Difficult Decisions with SmartSpectra
articles.description: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge           What I Built   "My gut...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge

What I Built

"My gut says..." How many times have you said that about a choice you couldn't make? Move to another city for a job, or stay. Study abroad, or start working. Say the hard thing to someone, or keep the peace. I have said it about all three, and I could never tell you what my gut was actually saying.

CrossRoads is a Windows desktop app for that moment. You type your two options. Then, for about four minutes, you imagine living each one, twice, in a mirrored order (A, B, B, A), while a camera reads your pulse through the Presage SmartSpectra SDK. At the end you get a mirror, not a verdict: which option your body stayed calmer with, the moment that moved you most, and a few questions to sit with.

The answer shows which way your body leaned:

  • One option kept you calmer, and the other made you tenser. CrossRoads names which one, and asks whether that tension was fear or excitement.
  • Or both felt the same to your body. Then the choice is about what you value, not what you fear. That is an answer too.

The idea is inspired by the somatic marker hypothesis: the body reacts to options before the mind can explain why. CrossRoads makes those reactions visible. It is for life decisions, never for health or treatment decisions, and it is a reflection tool, not medical advice.

Demo

A real check: imagining telling my parents, while my pulse climbs.

Try it without a camera or a key: download CrossRoads from the GitHub Release and click Try the sample. It opens a real session I recorded and replays it. (Windows may show "Windows protected your PC" because the app is not code-signed: choose More info, then Run anyway.)

Code

github.com/PawanBhandari03/smartspectra-challenge (MIT). The README has the run-from-source steps (Windows 10/11, Node 20+, npm install, npm start, plus a free Presage API key) and a "How judges can test" section. The Windows installer and a portable version are on the Release page.

How It Responds to Human Signals

What it reads. CrossRoads asks the SDK for seven measurements: chest and abdomen breathing, breathing rate, pulse, HRV, blinks and expressions. Pulse decides the result; breathing, blinks and expressions are shown live alongside it.

How it responds live. The session screen draws your pulse for the last 40 seconds in the colour of the option you are imagining, a heart beats at your measured rate, and the camera check tells you in plain words when the light is too low or the frame rate is too slow. The SDK runs in Electron's main process with native camera capture and a preload bridge to the screens.

What building it taught me. My first version imagined each option once and compared it with a calm baseline. Two lessons came quickly. First, only 10 frames per second reached the SDK, which needs 25 or more: the window-based mode copied about 3.6 MB per frame. Native capture in the main process fixed it, and a phone used as a webcam held a steady 30 fps. Second, I ran a control that should show nothing, tea vs coffee, and it showed a bigger difference than a real decision: the body drifts during a session, and with one visit per option that drift looks like a preference.

The method. So each option is now visited twice in a mirrored order (A B B A, or B A A B), and the two options are compared with each other, which cancels the drift. For each visit CrossRoads takes the median of reliable pulse readings: stable, confidence of at least 50, skipping the first 15 seconds while the reading settles, ignoring readings for 10 seconds after a signal dropout, and dropping physically impossible jumps. A calmer option is named when both rounds agree and each difference beats max(the visit-to-visit wobble, 6 bpm). I tuned that 6 bpm on my own recordings: a resting pulse can drift 6 to 9 bpm from one minute to the next by itself, so CrossRoads only speaks up when the difference is bigger than that, in both rounds.

Tested on real decisions (daylight, a phone camera):

Decision Gap in round 1 Gap in round 2 What CrossRoads said
Tea vs coffee (a control with nothing to find) 5.0 bpm 3.9 bpm Neutral, exactly as it should be
A quiet afternoon at the beach vs giving a speech to 1,000 people 10.0 bpm 8.1 bpm Calmer with the beach
Telling my parents I want a different career vs keeping the path they chose 10.7 bpm 9.4 bpm Calmer with keeping the path (87% stable readings)
Staying in my city vs moving to Bangalore 0.3 bpm 0.3 bpm, the other way No side: a values decision for me
A master's abroad vs starting work 2.1 bpm 8.0 bpm, the other way No side, but it pointed to the moment that moved me most: +8.4 bpm at "what did you give up for it?"

The numbers for every session are in docs/VALIDATION.md.

Built to be testable. A free replay mode plays recorded sessions as if live, which mattered because the free trial gave 100 credits (a four-minute check costs about 8). Signal Lab shows the raw SDK output. 48 automated tests run on every push.

Prize Categories

I am entering all three: Best Overall Human-Sensing Experience, Most Creative or Delightful Use and Best Thoughtful Real-World Use. (An entry can be considered for all three, but can win only once.)

Best Overall Human-Sensing Experience. The whole experience is built from a person's real-time signal. Your pulse is drawn live in the colour of the option you are imagining, a heart beats at your measured rate, and the result is made of how that pulse changed between two options. It is tested against a control and a calm-vs-stress scene, so the response to the signal is meaningful, not decorative.

Most Creative or Delightful Use. I wanted a camera vital-signs SDK to help with a human question instead of a fitness or stress score. The result screen is a crossroads that draws itself in, with the calmer path thickening (or both staying equal when your body didn't pick a side). The look is a warm paper-and-ink "decision journal", with a dark mode. After a check you can save your decision and a share card: a picture of the answer with the option you chose and no pulse numbers.

Best Thoughtful Real-World Use. The need is common: people stuck between two options who want to reflect, not be told. CrossRoads is designed around consent and trust. Consent sits beside the options with a required tick. There is a REC badge and live preview whenever the camera measures, a "Hide me" blur, and a Focus mode that hides the live numbers. Data stays on your computer and can be deleted. The sample works without a camera or key, and the app says up front, in plain words, if a live check needs a key.

Consent and Data Handling

  • Consent. Before any measurement, a card beside the two options explains what happens and asks for an explicit tick. The camera is on only during the camera check and the session. A REC badge and live preview show when it measures. You can stop at any time. If imagining an option feels upsetting, stop and take a break.
  • Storage. CrossRoads stores numbers (pulse, breathing, blinks, expression scores), your two options and an optional note, on your own computer. CrossRoads never saves or uploads your video. It asks the SDK for only seven measurements, and a test fails if that list grows. Your Presage API key is stored encrypted with Windows safeStorage and is never in the download.
  • Sharing. CrossRoads shares nothing automatically. "Save as image" writes a picture only where you choose, and it contains no pulse numbers.
  • Retention and deletion. Data is kept until you delete it. You can delete one check from My decisions, delete everything or remove the key in Settings. Uninstalling leaves the data folder in place.
  • What the SDK contacts. When a live session starts, the SmartSpectra SDK contacts Presage to check the API key and credits, authorise the requested measurements, register the device and download its models. SDK telemetry is switched off.
  • AI services and tracking. The app uses no AI service, has no accounts and no analytics.
  • Not medical. CrossRoads is a general wellness and reflection tool. It makes no diagnosis or treatment claims and is meant for one person reflecting on their own decision, never for monitoring anyone else.
  • Best results. Daylight on your face and a steady camera. Windows 10/11.

Built with the Presage SmartSpectra SDK, Electron, esbuild and electron-builder, and the Newsreader typeface (SIL Open Font License) via Fontsource.

Your head has arguments for both sides. Your body has something to say too. CrossRoads shows it. A mirror, not a verdict.

articles.title: Here Lie My Side Projects.
articles.description: I did not plan a funeral. I opened a folder.  It was a Sunday, the kind where the light comes in...
articles.body_html:
I did not plan a funeral. I opened a folder.

It was a Sunday, the kind where the light comes in sideways and you can hear the neighbours' television through the wall, and I was looking for a file I had lost. A photo, actually. A screenshot of a receipt I needed. I never found it. I found the graveyard instead. That is how it goes with folders. You go in looking for one thing and come out carrying something else. Inside the folder called "projects" were four folders I had not opened in months, and one I had never opened at all. I sat there for a minute, looking at them, and then I counted. Four projects. Four starts. Four endings I never noticed happening.

So I walked through them, one by one, the way you walk through a graveyard when you have nowhere else to be. Each one has a stone. Here they are.

HABITRACK — March to March.
Cause of death: the settings page.
Last words: "fix streak counter (again)"

This was the first one, and the one I loved most. The idea was simple: a page where you tick off your habits and watch a little flame grow. I built the flame first. Of course I built the flame first. The flame was orange and it flickered when you ticked a box, and for three days I was the kind of person who ticks boxes. The flame had three sizes. Small for three days, medium for seven, big for thirty. I never saw big. Nobody saw big. Big is still in the code, waiting, like a room nobody has ever slept in. I used it myself for nine days. Nine days of morning walks and water and reading before bed, and then I missed a day. One day, a Tuesday, nothing dramatic, I just forgot. And the flame went out, and I could not face lighting it again. The flame was supposed to keep me going. Instead it kept score. I opened the settings page to add a "forgive one missed day" button, saw what the settings page needed, toggles, defaults, a whole second app hiding inside the first one, and closed the laptop. That was March. The streak counter is still broken. The commit message says "(again)" because I had fixed it twice before, and both times it broke in a new way, and the third time I wrote "(again)" the way you sigh in text form.

THE RECIPE BOX — June to July.
Cause of death: the login form.
Last words: "add search (basic)"

Twelve recipes. All mine. The lentil soup, the fried rice, the chicken curry I make when people come over and I want them to think I have my life together. I photographed every dish, in my own kitchen, on my own chipped plate. The photos were the fun part. The search box was the fun part too. Type "lentil" and the soup appears, like a trick. Then I realised that if anyone else was ever going to use it, they would need an account, and accounts need passwords, and passwords need reset emails, and reset emails need a whole machine I did not want to build. I sat there one evening, looking at the login form I had started — two empty boxes and a button that did nothing — and I understood something I did not want to understand: I did not want to build the login form. I wanted to cook the soup. I closed the laptop and cooked the soup. The search still says "(basic)" in the commit message. The search was fine. The search was never the problem.

BUDGET BUDDY — September to September.
Cause of death: the bank statement.
Last words: "wip: csv import"

This one died the fastest, and I respect it for that. The idea: upload your bank statement, see where your money goes, feel like an adult. The fun part was the pie chart. I made a pie chart with seven colours and I stared at it for a long time, the way you stare at a cake you baked yourself. Then I tried to import a real statement, and the bank's file had columns in an order I had never seen, and dates in a format from another century, and one row that just said "MISC" with no amount at all. I spent a Saturday afternoon writing code to understand one bank's idea of a spreadsheet, and by the evening I had a headache and a new respect for accountants. The next morning I opened a plain spreadsheet, typed my spending into it by hand, and it took fourteen minutes. Fourteen minutes, and it worked. Budget Buddy is still in the folder, with its beautiful pie chart and its one broken import. The spreadsheet has no pie chart. The spreadsheet works.

FLASHCARDS — October to November.
Cause of death: card number thirteen.
Last words: "add deck: spanish basics (12 cards)"

The flip animation was the whole project, if I am honest. A card that turns over when you tap it, smooth as a coin trick. I built the flip in an evening and showed it to everyone I knew. Then I had to fill it with cards, and filling it meant typing, and typing meant sitting down and typing two hundred words I did not know into little boxes. I got to twelve. Twelve cards of Spanish basics: hola, gracias, buenos días, and nine more I have mostly forgotten. I remember three now. Hola, gracias, and buenos días. The card that killed it was number thirteen. I sat there, looking at the empty box, and I could not think of a thirteenth word. Not because I did not know one. Because I knew that after thirteen would come fourteen, and after fourteen, a hundred and eighty-six more. I closed the laptop. The flip animation still works. It is beautiful. It flips twelve cards.

There was a fifth. It has one commit, called "initial commit," and no stone. Some projects do not even get a funeral. I do not remember what it was supposed to be. The folder is called "notes-app-final-v2." The name is the whole story. Final. Version two. There was a version one, and it is not in the folder, and I do not remember deleting it.

I sat with the graveyard for a while. Four stones, one unmarked, and a folder full of almosts. Then I did something I had not planned. I opened the oldest one, Habitrack, March, the flame, and I fixed the streak counter. Really fixed it, not the "(again)" kind. It took twenty minutes. Twenty minutes, for a bug I had carried around for eight months. Then I added the button I had never built: "forgive one missed day." One button. No settings page. No toggles. Just a button that says: it is fine. You missed a day. The flame stays lit.

I sat with the link for a while before I sent it. Sending it felt bigger than building it had, which is a strange thing to feel about a page with one button and a flame. But I sent it anyway. Three friends. No announcement, no launch, no post about it. Just a message: "I made this ages ago. It's ugly. It works. Don't judge the flame."

That evening, Rafi sent me a screenshot. Seven days. A little flame, lit, on his phone. "Day 7," he wrote. "Still going."

I looked at the screenshot for a long time. The flame was lit. Just not on my phone.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: Arcane: A Developer's Guide to the Open-Source Docker Management UI
articles.description: If you run Docker on more than one machine, you probably know the routine: SSH into a box, cd into a...
articles.body_html:
If you run Docker on more than one machine, you probably know the routine: SSH into a box, cd into a folder, docker compose ps, tail some logs, repeat on the next server. It works, but it does not scale well once you have a handful of hosts and a few dozen stacks.

Arcane is an open-source, self-hosted web UI for Docker and Docker Compose that tries to fix that without making you learn a new orchestration model. It sits on top of the Docker you already have and gives you a dashboard, a Compose editor, logs, a terminal, and multi-host management from one place.

This article covers what Arcane is, how to get it running, and the details that matter when you move past "it works on my laptop."

What Arcane is (and is not)

Arcane is:

  • A web UI for Docker and Compose. Containers, images, volumes, networks, and Compose "projects" (stacks) are all first-class.
  • Self-hosted, single container. You run it next to your workloads and talk to Docker through the socket (or a socket proxy).
  • Open source under BSD-3-Clause. No paid tiers, no feature gating.
  • Built with Go and SvelteKit. The backend is Go, the frontend is SvelteKit with TypeScript.

Arcane is not:

  • An orchestrator. It does not replace Kubernetes or Swarm scheduling. It manages Docker and Compose the way you already use them.
  • A new config format. Your stacks stay as normal compose.yaml files on disk. If you stop using Arcane tomorrow, docker compose up -d still works.

That last point is the main reason a lot of developers are trying it. There is no lock-in. Arcane reads and writes standard Compose files.

Feature overview

Here is what you get out of the box:

Area What you get
Containers Start, stop, restart, inspect, real-time logs, web terminal, process list
Compose projects Create and edit stacks in the browser, deploy, pull, redeploy
Images Browse, pull, prune, browse registry repos and tags, build workspace
Networks Management plus an interactive network topology view
Multi-host Manage remote Docker hosts through agents (direct or edge mode)
GitOps Point Arcane at a Git repo and sync stacks from it
Updates Tag-based auto-updates with an optional cool-down delay
Security Trivy vulnerability scanning, image patching with Copacetic
Auth Local users, OIDC/SSO, passkeys, MFA, role mappings
Ops Scheduled volume and S3 backups, OpenTelemetry export
Automation REST API and a Go-based CLI (arcane-cli)
Runtimes Docker, plus Podman (rootful, rootless, and quadlets)

Quick start

You need Docker and Docker Compose on the host.

1. Generate an encryption key

Arcane requires a 32-byte ENCRYPTION_KEY. Either of these works:

openssl rand -hex 32

docker run --rm ghcr.io/getarcaneapp/manager:v2 /app/arcane generate secret

2. Create compose.yaml 

services:
  arcane:
    image: ghcr.io/getarcaneapp/manager:v2
    container_name: arcane
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "3552:3552"
    environment:
      - APP_URL=http://localhost:3552
      - ENCRYPTION_KEY=replace-with-your-generated-key
      - PROJECTS_DIRECTORY=/opt/stacks
      - TZ=UTC
    volumes:
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock
      - arcane-data:/app/data
      - /opt/stacks:/opt/stacks

volumes:
  arcane-data:

3. Start it 

docker compose up -d

Open http://<your-host>:3552 and log in with the default credentials:

  • Username: arcane
  • Password: arcane-admin

You will be forced to change the password on first login.

Things developers should know

The quick start gets you running. These are the details that save you time later.

1. Use the current image name and pin v2

The image moved from ghcr.io/getarcaneapp/arcane to ghcr.io/getarcaneapp/manager. Many older blog posts and templates still use the old name. Official mirrors also exist on Docker Hub (getarcaneapp/manager) and Quay (quay.io/getarcaneapp/manager).

Pin the v2 tag for anything you care about. Avoid latest and any beta tags in production.

2. Keep host and container paths identical for stacks

Notice the stacks volume above: /opt/stacks:/opt/stacks. Compose files often use relative paths for bind mounts (./data:/data). When Arcane runs docker compose from inside its container, those paths are resolved against the Docker host, not the Arcane container.

Arcane can translate mismatched paths now, but mounting the same path on both sides is still the recommended setup and avoids surprises. PROJECTS_DIRECTORY also accepts a <containerPath>:<hostPath> form if you need them to differ.

3. Mounting the Docker socket is root-equivalent

Anything with access to /var/run/docker.sock can effectively control the host. That is true for Arcane and for every other Docker UI.

For hardened setups, put a socket proxy in front of Docker and point Arcane at it:

environment:
  - DOCKER_HOST=tcp://docker-socket-proxy:2375

Then remove the socket mount from the Arcane service. Two common proxies are wollomatic/socket-proxy (deny-by-default) and Tecnativa/docker-socket-proxy. Take the exact allow-list from Arcane's socket proxy docs rather than guessing.

One gotcha: if you use wollomatic/socket-proxy with -allowfrom, include arcane-upgrader as well as arcane. Self-upgrades run through a helper with that alias and will fail without it.

4. Every secret supports _FILE

Any sensitive variable can be read from a file by adding _FILE. This plays well with Docker secrets:

environment:
  - ENCRYPTION_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/arcane_encryption_key
secrets:
  - arcane_encryption_key

Also note that JWT_SECRET from older guides is no longer used in 2.x. Arcane generates and stores its own session signing key. If you still set JWT_SECRET, you just get a warning at startup, so remove it.

5. Behind a reverse proxy, set TRUSTED_PROXIES and APP_URL

If Arcane sits behind Nginx, Traefik, Caddy, or a Cloudflare Tunnel:

  • Set APP_URL to the public URL (for example https://arcane.example.com, no port).
  • Set TRUSTED_PROXIES to the CIDR of your proxy. Without it, client IPs in logs and rate limiting will be wrong.
  • Make sure WebSockets are passed through. Logs and the terminal depend on them. In Nginx that means proxy_http_version 1.1 plus the Upgrade and Connection "upgrade" headers.

Minimal Nginx location block:

location / {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3552;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
}

Arcane can also serve HTTPS itself with TLS_ENABLED, TLS_CERT_FILE, and TLS_KEY_FILE if you prefer not to run a proxy.

6. Managing multiple hosts: direct vs edge agents

To manage other servers, run the Arcane agent (ghcr.io/getarcaneapp/agent) on each one. There are two modes:

  • Direct mode. The manager connects to the agent on TCP port 3553. Simple, but the agent must be reachable from the manager.
  • Edge mode. The agent dials out to the manager over mTLS. No inbound port is needed on the remote host, which makes it a good fit for machines behind NAT or a home router.

You do not need to write the agent config by hand. In the UI, go to Environments > Add Environment and Arcane generates a token and a ready-to-paste Compose snippet.

Edge agents support several transports through EDGE_TRANSPORT:

  • auto (default): gRPC tunnel with WebSocket fallback
  • grpc or websocket: force one tunnel type
  • poll: periodic check-in with no persistent tunnel, useful behind Cloudflare Tunnel or strict proxies

An agent in poll mode shows as Standby when idle. That is normal and means it is healthy.

If you run Traefik in front of the manager with edge agents on auto or grpc, disable the entrypoint read timeout, otherwise tunnels drop after about 60 seconds.

7. GitOps without a CI pipeline

You can point Arcane at a Git repository that contains your Compose files and it will keep the stacks in sync. For small teams and home labs this is often enough to get a "push to deploy" flow without setting up webhooks or a CI runner. Use SSH_KNOWN_HOSTS to pin host keys when cloning over SSH.

8. Auto-updates with a safety delay

Arcane can update containers when a new image is published for the tag you track. To reduce the risk of pulling a compromised or broken image the minute it lands, you can set an update delay in hours.

Per project, in your Compose file:

x-arcane:
  updater:
    delay: 72

Or per container, with a label:

labels:
  - com.getarcaneapp.arcane.updater.delay=72

A value of 0 on a service opts it out of the delay.

9. Automate it: API and CLI

Arcane exposes a REST API, and there is a Go CLI for scripting:

go install github.com/getarcaneapp/arcane/cli/v2@latest

For automation, ADMIN_STATIC_API_KEY lets you provision a fixed API key through the environment instead of creating one in the UI.

10. Use SSO if you share it with a team

OIDC is configured under Settings > Authentication or through environment variables (OIDC_ENABLED, OIDC_CLIENT_ID, OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET, OIDC_ISSUER_URL, OIDC_SCOPES). The redirect URI is:

https://<your-arcane-url>/auth/oidc/callback

You can map IdP group claims to Arcane roles with OIDC_ROLE_MAPPINGS, including per-environment roles. If you ever lock yourself out, a local backup login is available at /login/backup.

A small but common mistake: when you use the list form of environment: in Compose, do not wrap OIDC values in quotes. The quotes become part of the value and discovery fails.

Useful environment variables

Variable Purpose Default
ENCRYPTION_KEY Required 32-byte key for encrypting stored secrets none
APP_URL Public URL of the UI http://localhost:3552
PROJECTS_DIRECTORY Where Compose projects live /app/data/projects
DOCKER_HOST Docker endpoint, use tcp:// for a socket proxy unix:///var/run/docker.sock
PUID / PGID User and group the app runs as 65532
TRUSTED_PROXIES CIDR of reverse proxies unset
DATABASE_URL Database connection SQLite
TLS_ENABLED Serve HTTPS directly false
LOG_LEVEL Log verbosity info
TZ Time zone system

If the container cannot talk to the Docker socket because of permissions, either run it as root or add the host's docker group ID with group_add.

How it compares

Arcane overlaps with tools like Portainer, Dockge, and Komodo. A rough way to think about it:

  • Portainer is the long-standing, broad option, with some features in paid editions.
  • Dockge focuses narrowly on Compose stack editing on a single host.
  • Arcane aims for a modern UI with Compose at the center, built-in multi-host agents, GitOps, security scanning, and SSO, all under a permissive open-source license with no paid tier.

The best choice depends on how many hosts you run and how much you want built in. Arcane is easy to try side by side with whatever you use now, since it works on plain Compose files.

Links:

  • Repository: https://github.com/getarcaneapp/arcane

If you try it, share your setup in the comments. I am curious how people are running it across multiple hosts.
