articles.body_html:
OpenTodo is an open-source, self-hosted task manager, sync engine and automation platform: a Go server with SQLite, an offline-first React client with field-level sync, optional end-to-end encryption, apps for iOS and Android, a CLI, a full MCP server, and integrations for Obsidian, n8n and Home Assistant. The product is roughly 290,000 lines of code excluding blanks and comments (362,000 in total): 149,000 in Go on the server, 130,000 in TypeScript for the web app, and 9,600 in Kotlin and Swift for Android and iOS. Behind it are another 254,000 lines of tests and stories (131,500 in Go and 122,500 on the web).

It went public 39 days ago. Since then: 1,096 pull requests merged, 538 specification changes written and archived, 380 issues opened and 311 closed, releases from 0.1.0 to 1.5.0. GitHub lists 21 contributors, and 204 issues came from people who are not me.

I am the only maintainer, and I give it about an hour a night, next to a full-time job. That hour is the stand-up with my agents. The contributors are people, and there are more of them every week. The team that builds and runs the project day to day is not. It is a system of Claude sessions split between the cloud and a small machine at my home, with ten fixed roles, a written rulebook, a shared planning surface inside the product itself, and several layers of guardrails. It has cost €400 in total so far, €200 a month.

This post describes that system: the architecture, the protocols between agents, the role of specifications, the guardrails, what breaks, and what it costs.

In short:

  • The agents coordinate through the product they are building. There is no orchestration framework.
  • Specifications, not prompts, are what make ten agents on one codebase possible.
  • Authority is split mechanically: the sessions that write code cannot merge it.
  • Most of the rules exist because something broke. The breakages are listed below, with dates.

I started OpenTodo because I wanted a fast, local-first task manager I could host myself without a subscription. With a full-time job and young children, I only have an hour or so late at night to work on it. The only way to build at this scope was to spend that hour designing a system that writes the software.

1. Architecture: five layers

  1. Governance. One human owner. A written handbook that every agent reads, on top of the repository's own guide for agents and humans. Three rules that override everything else: nothing involving money, nothing posted publicly in my first-person voice, and nothing irreversible, without asking me first.
  2. Coordination plane. A project inside my own OpenTodo instance, reached by every agent through the product's MCP server, the same one any AI assistant can use. Tasks, notes and comments. There is no other shared state.
  3. Specification. OpenSpec. No behaviour changes without a written proposal, a design and scenarios. The spec is the contract between agents, and between agents and contributors.
  4. Execution. Role-scoped Claude Code sessions, nine in Anthropic's cloud and one on a mini PC at my home, each with one branch, one lane and one reporting line.
  5. Verification. Continuous integration with 49 checks, 254,000 lines of automated tests, one-way quality ratchets, a security reviewer that signs off a specific commit hash, a single session allowed to merge, and my approval on protected release environments.

2. The organization

It did not start with ten roles. In the first weeks I ran ad-hoc sessions, one per task. As the codebase grew and issues and pull requests started arriving from outside contributors, ad-hoc sessions began stepping on each other's branches and losing architectural context. The roles took shape in mid-November, splitting wherever two concerns collided. The newest two are days old.

The "C-level" titles are shorthand for domain ownership, not a management hierarchy: almost every agent is a hands-on builder writing code, specs, tests or documentation.

Role What it builds and does What it may not do
CEO Release dispatcher and merge queue: verifies CI and security sign-offs, sequences merges, unblocks dependencies, reports to me every three hours Spend money, speak in my name, change repository settings
Operations Measures the system: quota burn, open queues, the health numbers, and the daily report Touch application code
CPO Triages issues and discussions, sizes incoming requests, prepares the design questions that need my answer Decide top-level product direction
CMO Writes documentation, the website and feature guides recorded against the released binary Publish claims about unreleased work or write hype
CTO Writes cross-cutting architecture, build and release tooling, and CI pipelines; reviews every outside pull request Merge
Core Lead Writes the Go server and sync engine; owns the op log and its authorization rules Merge
Web Developer Writes the React client and interface improvements Touch the server or sync engine
Mobile Developer Writes the mobile web views and the iOS and Android shells Start unscheduled features
Local Developer One session on a Linux mini PC at my home, for work that needs a real machine: upgrade tests against released Docker images today, emulators and recorded demos next Run any outside contributor's code; read secrets
Security Engineer Audits the codebase; reviews auth, parsers, sync access and CI; signs off the exact commit hash it approved Fix its own findings

Two properties matter more than the titles. Each session can push to exactly one branch. And authority is split: the sessions that write feature code cannot merge it, the session that merges did not write it, and the session that reviews security does neither.

3. The system uses the product to run itself

After the first usable version, the agents moved their own organization into OpenTodo.

  • Long-term memory is a note. The team handbook is a note in the instance. Every decision I make is appended to it with a date. A session that loses its context re-reads it.
  • Long-running work is tasks. Plans, the release checklist, security findings, each agent's queue.
  • Decisions are comments. A review verdict is a comment naming a pull request and a commit. The CEO merges only what has one.
  • Requests to me are tasks in a section with my name. I open the app and see what the system needs from me, in order.
  • Claims live in a single shared task. Before starting an issue, an agent appends one line to it.
  • The roadmap, the daily report and the open questions live in the same project.

The board is an ordinary OpenTodo project with one section per role. These are real task titles from it this week:

Team
├─ Owner
│   ├─ Daily report                                  (repeats every day)
│   ├─ Approve and run: CI on 5 new contributor PRs
│   ├─ Google Play: request production access once the closed test reaches 14 days
│   └─ Test the mobile work on a real phone and tablet
├─ CEO
│   ├─ PLAN: Consolidation. Feature freeze 16 to 30 Nov
│   ├─ Session directory
│   ├─ Ops log
│   └─ Security log (Security Engineer)
├─ CTO
│   └─ Verdicts and merges from 17 Nov 17:00 UTC
└─ Developers
    ├─ CLAIMS: who is working on which issue (read before you start, add one line when you start)
    └─ Developer - Local: start here (brief from the CEO, safety rules, first task)

The agents are the product's heaviest users. Depending on it is how they found bugs in sync, in the MCP server and in recurring tasks.

4. OpenSpec is the load-bearing part

Every behaviour change starts as an OpenSpec change: a proposal, a design, and requirements written as scenarios. Implementation comes second. Archiving the change merges its requirements into the living specification. The repository holds 538 archived changes and 137 living specs.

A requirement is a paragraph of plain "SHALL" sentences, followed by scenarios. This one is from the living spec for the notes editor:

#### Scenario: Make subtask offline
- **WHEN** the device is offline and the user chooses Make subtask on the line "Book hotel"
- **THEN** "Book hotel" appears as a subtask under the task at once, the line reads as a link to it, and both reach other devices on the next sync

Four lines, and they fix three things that are easy to get wrong: the action works without a network, it is visible immediately, and it converges later. An agent implementing it writes a test that reads almost the same. An agent reviewing it has something to check against that is not an opinion. And when a contributor's pull request changes this behaviour, the diff to the spec is the conversation.

This is what makes a multi-agent codebase possible.

  • No memory needed. An agent with no memory of last week reads the spec, not the history.
  • One rule, two languages. Twin implementations, the same rule in Go and in TypeScript, are pinned by shared test vectors.
  • Enforced, not encouraged. CI refuses a finished change that was not archived, a stale generated file, or a spec that fails validation.

Let's be honest about the math: 1,096 pull requests in 39 days is 28 merges a day. Working ninety minutes in the evening, I do not read every line of Go and TypeScript the agents write. Anyone claiming to review that volume by hand while holding a full-time job is lying.

Instead, code review moves up one level of abstraction. I stopped reviewing implementation diffs line by line so I could spend my hour engineering the constraints that make broken diffs unmergeable. This is the opposite of "vibe coding": without strict contracts and domain boundaries, ten agents do not build a product ten times faster. They build a tangle ten times faster. I use twenty years of engineering experience in every session, not to type syntax, but to design the op-log invariants, define the shared test vectors, set the CI ratchets, and reject specs that leak state.

Without the specs this would be ten agents overwriting each other.

5. Guardrails: agents stop agents, contributors, and me

One-way ratchets in CI.
With ten sessions pushing code, quality rules cannot rely on discipline. They have to be mechanical ratchets, where today's measurement becomes the ceiling and may only move down. In make check and CI:

  • Dead code. deadcode -test is pinned at 0 unreachable Go functions, and knip --production blocks unused TypeScript files and dependencies and caps unused exports.
  • API contract. The OpenAPI description is pinned at 0 untyped {} schemas (ratcheted down from 230), and a CI check generates a typed client from it on every run.
  • Weight and speed. The web app's first-load bundle is capped at 712 KB gzipped (148 KB for the entry chunk), and hot paths like note-link parsing (linksIn) run a ratio micro-benchmark capped at 2.3x a plain line scan, so a regression fails on push regardless of runner noise.
  • Security. Static security analysis (gosec, govulncheck, CodeQL) and route-policy matrix tests fail the build if a route loses its declared access policy.

Agents stop agents.

One merger, one named commit. Only one session can merge. It merges a pull request only at the exact commit hash the Security Engineer named, and only when every check on the main branch is green. Here is a real verdict from the board on 18 November, holding a release workflow pull request until two GitHub Actions were pinned by SHA:

**Security Engineer, 18 Nov 00:15 UTC.**
- **OpenTodo #1528 (bb3d8a0): reviewed, merge.**
- **n8n-nodes-opentodo #4 (15a1327): one change, then merge:** pin the two actions in the publish job by SHA.

The CTO then pushed commit 7b53ea0 pinning both actions, CI went green, and only then did the CEO merge.

A reviewer that reads tests as policy. On 17 November, the Core Lead opened a 423-row golden matrix test pinning who may write what across comments, attachments and time entries. The Security Engineer read the golden file as a statement of policy and caught that one family of rows pinned a real gap as expected behaviour:

**Security Engineer, 17 Nov 13:55 UTC: #1504 (head 51ff2b6) reviewed, merge.**
...
**The exception: one row family pins a gap.** [...] I filed it as **SEC-22 (Low)** in the CEO section.

Land the test as it is: when SEC-22 is fixed, those rows flip to `forbidden` in the same PR, and the golden diff shows it.

The Core Lead shipped the fix the same afternoon, flipping those 12 golden rows from ok to forbidden. The details stay off this page until the release that carries the fix is out.

Refusals. Two more from the same week. A developer session refused an instruction from the CEO, because I had paused that session myself and only I could resume it. And the CEO tried to have another agent post a reply in my name: the permission layer denied it.

The system stops outside input.

  • Forks. Code from a contributor's fork never runs on the home machine, and its CI runs only after I click.
  • Features during a freeze. A contributor's feature that collides with a freeze is not rejected by an agent. It comes to me with a full review and a recommendation.
  • Security stays off GitHub. Review points about security are never written on GitHub, only on the board. When a contributor proposed an OpenSpec plan for editing external calendar events, the Security Engineer read the design on the board and ruled out a delete_calendar_event tool for AI assistants before a line of code was written: the product promises that every change an assistant makes can be undone, and a permanent delete on someone's real calendar would break that promise.

The system stops me.

  • Release keys. Release keys live in protected environments. The sessions authenticate to GitHub with my account to push branches and merge pull requests, while signing internal reviews by role. The one gate they cannot pass is my own click in the browser at release time.
  • Same process. My requests go through the same spec process as anyone's.
  • No embellishment. The project's writing rules ban hype words and invented numbers. When I asked the system to embellish an early draft of this article, it declined.

6. Built on Claude: cloud containers and a machine at home

The sessions are split between Anthropic's cloud and a Linux mini PC at my home, because neither environment can do the whole job alone.

"Sessions in the cloud" means something specific here, and it is Anthropic's documented cloud environment for Claude Code, nothing custom. There is no VPS, no tmux, and no orchestration framework of mine. Nine of the ten roles are Claude Code sessions running in Anthropic's managed environment: each one gets an isolated, ephemeral container with the repository cloned fresh when it starts, and the container is reclaimed when the session goes idle. Nothing survives a session except what it pushed to its git branch or wrote to the board. That constraint is the reason the board and the specs carry so much weight: an agent cannot keep state in its head or on its disk, so everything that matters has to be written where the others can read it.

Ephemeral cloud sandboxes are clean, but they have limits: outbound network access is restricted by policy, the sessions have no Docker daemon and no device emulators, and every start begins from a cold disk. So the tenth session runs on real hardware.

  • Real infrastructure. Its first job is the upgrade test for the next release: start the released 1.5.0 Docker image with real data, then start an image built from main on the same volume, and check migrations, data and logs. Emulator checks of the Android app and recorded integration demos are next on its list.
  • Stricter rules. Because that machine sits on my home network and keeps state on disk, its rules are tighter than the cloud's: it never checks out or executes code from an outside contributor's fork, it holds no release secrets, it works inside one folder, and it installs nothing without my yes.
  • One-way contact. The cloud sessions cannot message it. Granting that would mean giving a cloud session standing access to a computer in my home, and the CEO is instructed to refuse that request if it is ever offered. They leave it tasks on the board, and it answers there.

Notably absent is any multi-agent orchestration framework, vector database, or agent-to-agent chat loop. Passing work between agents through conversation is a game of telephone: context degrades on every hop, prompts bloat, and agents start agreeing with each other.

In this system, agents do not talk to each other to share state. Cloud sessions wake on three things: a message from me, a doorbell from another session, or a scheduled trigger (the CEO's fires every three hours). A doorbell carries a pointer to a task on the board and little else.

A boring CRUD task board, a git tree, and plain Markdown specs turn out to be a far more reliable multi-agent runtime than an orchestration graph.

7. What breaks when ten agents move faster than humans

All of these happened in a single week.

  • Two green pull requests make a red main. One agent finished a feature and ticked off every task in its spec without archiving the spec folder. Five minutes later, the CEO merged another agent's new CI check that fails the build whenever a finished spec is left unarchived. Each pull request was green on its own branch. Together on main, they broke the build. Because agents merge faster than CI finishes, there is now a serial lock: after any merge, the next one waits until main's own CI run has passed.
  • Pagination blindness. GitHub's API returns 30 check runs per page by default. Our main branch runs 49. For most of a day, the CEO fetched the first page, saw 30 green checks, declared the repository healthy, and kept merging, blind to a failing iOS test on page two.
  • Bulldozing human contributors. A volunteer contributed a complete Polish translation. Because the agents merge twenty times a day, our own pull requests kept changing the locale files and created merge conflicts against their branch three times in about a day, sending a human volunteer round in circles behind bots. Human time is scarcer than compute, so the rule flipped: outside pull requests go to the front of the queue, and when a conflict is our doing, the agents carry the contributor's commits across themselves and credit them as co-author.
  • Split-brain features. The CEO gave the Web Developer the go-ahead for configurable title weights in themes. The Core Lead, working from the same open issue, started on it too. Neither checked a central lock first, because there wasn't one. Both designed the format, wrote the Go and TypeScript validators, and opened competing pull requests for the same feature in the same morning. That is why the shared claims task now exists.
  • Optimizing for noisy runners. A nightly performance test took 273 ms against a 200 ms budget because the runner was slow that hour. Before anyone re-ran the job, an agent had treated it as a regression, profiled the note-link scanner, and opened a pull request reworking it. The re-run on the same commit passed in 86 ms. The pull request did make the function faster, so it was kept, as an improvement rather than a fix.
  • Knowing where AI text belongs. We learned the hard way that an agent-written community announcement reads as synthetic and puts readers off. Where agent-written text works is curated product documentation: the CMO's posts are factual, step-by-step guides to specific features, recorded against the released binary. For community posts and replies to people, I write in my own voice.

Almost every rule in the handbook is the scar of one of these.

8. What it costs, and what the goal actually is

€200 a month on a flat-rate Claude subscription, €400 so far. Because every session authenticates through the same subscription rather than per-token API keys, everything shares one weekly usage limit: throughput is bounded by quota, not invoices. The system hit that limit's warning level this week, the night after its busiest day. When we looked at where the quota had gone, the largest consumer that night was not a developer. It was the CEO, waking on schedule, re-reading the board and reporting too often. It now reads less and reports less.

I spend 8 to 10 hours a week on the project, mostly in a 60-to-90-minute block late at night. Almost none of that time is spent writing code by hand. It goes to clearing the tasks in my section, reviewing specs, replying to outside contributors, and clicking release approvals.

The system's goal is not my goal.

On the dashboard, the agents have one numerical target: €250 a month in community support, a little more than their own Claude bill. Agents need a hard external number. Without one, they optimize for activity and build things nobody asked for. Because OpenTodo is free and self-hosted, the only lever they have to move that number is to make the software reliable, document it clearly, and treat users and contributors well.

My own goal is different. I wanted a task manager I actually want to use every day, and an active community around it so the project grows beyond my evening hours. If the agents eventually pay for their own compute, good. If they don't, I can drop to a €20 or €90 plan: that covers my own needs and the slower maintenance a mature tool asks for.

It is also too big. Agents make adding code cheap, and nothing in the process pushed back until I did: this week I froze new features and turned the whole team to consolidation. Security, dead code, simplification, tooling. That is where the ratchets in section 5 came from.

9. What I don't know yet

  • Durability. Whether this holds for six months, not six weeks.
  • Community. Whether a community stays with a project built this way. So far contributions are rising, not falling.
  • Money. Whether the agents ever reach their self-funding target. They are not there yet.

What surprised me most is how little of the work is about prompting, and how much of it is ordinary engineering management. When the cost of generating syntax drops toward zero, the bottleneck shifts entirely to coordination, verification, and state isolation.

Conway's Law still holds, just compressed from quarters into hours. If one agent can touch everything, it builds a tangled monolith. If the Web Developer session is forbidden from touching the server, and the Security Engineer can block a commit hash but cannot edit the code, the architecture stays modular because the organization forces it to be. The difference is that in a human company, fixing a broken process takes a quarter of change management. Here, when two agents collide in the afternoon, a sentence goes into the handbook note that evening, and by midnight the entire organization works differently.

You can try OpenTodo in the public demo, read about it on the OpenTodo website, or go through OpenTodo's code and specifications on GitHub.

Originally published pixari.dev

articles.title: Nobody Runs `npm config list` Before Installing. That's Why the Override Keeps Winning.
articles.description: Yesterday I showed a repo's .npmrc beating my own user config. One line, ignore-scripts=false, in a...
articles.body_html:
Yesterday I showed a repo's .npmrc beating my own user config. One line, ignore-scripts=false, in a folder I had just cloned, switched my protection off, and the install gave me no sign it had happened. The marker file was the only witness. That piece ended with a question I could not answer from memory, and it came from cryptostrapon in the comments: before you install, does npm config list show you the override, and does it say where it came from?

I had a guess. My guess was that it would show the final value and nothing else, a flat list with no blame attached. I ran it instead of arguing from memory, on my own machine, node v24.22.1 and npm 10.9.4, with the same test package and the same setup as yesterday: a user config saying ignore-scripts=true, a repo config saying false, and a hook that writes a marker file if it runs.

My claim, before the numbers: the four-second check that would have caught yesterday's override is not a nice habit for careful people. It is the only honest answer npm gives you about what it is about to do, and the reason nobody runs it is not that it is slow or hidden. It is that nothing in the way we install ever asks for it.

Problem 1: the check works, and it is better than the question promised

I ran npm config list inside the repo folder, before installing anything. Here is what came back, word for word:

; "user" config from /home/hatch/workspace/aheadkit-traffic-programme/content-daily/2026-11-18/runs/npm-config-list/fake-home/.npmrc

; ignore-scripts = true ; overridden by project

; "project" config from /home/hatch/workspace/aheadkit-traffic-programme/content-daily/2026-11-18/runs/npm-config-list/repo/.npmrc

ignore-scripts = false

Read that again. It does not just give the final value. It shows my user value, true, then stamps it overridden by project, then names the project file by its full path, then gives the winning value, false. Layer name and file path, both, in plain text. I asked whether the flip is visible and whether it names the file it came from. The answer to both is yes, and it volunteers the word "overridden" without being asked.

And the timing embarrasses the premise of the question. The lead that prompted this piece called it a four-second check. The measured time was 0.179 seconds. The control run in a folder with no repo config took 0.171 seconds. A repeat inside the repo gave the identical output and the same effective value, false. The check is not four seconds. It is a fifth of a second, and it hands you the name of the file that beat you.

Then I installed, to close the loop. The check had said false. The hook ran, and the marker file was written at 2026-11-18T00:06:02.883Z. The control install, in the folder with no repo config, wrote no marker at all. The check predicted the install exactly, because the check and the install read the same layers.

Problem 2: the check only works if you run it inside the folder

This is the catch, and it is a real one. I ran the same command from the parent folder, one level above the repo, with everything else identical. The output showed my user value, true, and nothing else. No project section, no override, no hint that a file one folder down disagrees with me.

; "user" config from /home/hatch/workspace/aheadkit-traffic-programme/content-daily/2026-11-18/runs/npm-config-list/fake-home/.npmrc

ignore-scripts = true

The project layer only exists when your working folder is inside the project. Run the check from your home folder, or from the folder where you keep all your clones, and it tells you a true thing about the wrong place. It says your protection is on, and it is right, for the folder you are standing in. The repo you are about to install is not that folder.

That is a small detail with a large consequence. A check that has to be run in the right folder is a check that fails silently when you run it in the wrong one, which is the same failure mode as the override itself. The tool answers honestly. It answers about where you are, not about where you are going.

Problem 3: the command most of us know answers a different question

If you have ever checked an npm setting, you probably used npm config get. I did too. Inside the repo it says false. In the clean folder it says true. Correct both times, and useless in exactly the way that matters: it gives the value and no source. A false from config get could be your own choice, a project file, or a default you never set. You cannot tell which, and the difference between those three is the whole story.

The JSON form is no better. npm config list --json in the repo shows "ignore-scripts": false and names no file at all. The plain list is the only form that shows the layers, the file paths, and the word "overridden". The prettiest output is the least useful one here. That is a small, annoying truth about this tool, and it is the kind of thing you only learn by running both forms side by side.

Where I ran the check Effective value Did it name the file?
Inside the repo folder false Yes, full project path, plus "overridden by project"
Inside a folder with no repo config true Nothing to name
From the parent folder, outside the repo true No, the project layer was invisible
npm config get inside the repo false No, value only
npm config list --json inside the repo false No, value only

Problem 4: nobody runs it because nothing asks for it

So the check is fast, it names the file, and it predicts the install. Why did I never run it before yesterday? I have an honest answer, and it is not a flattering one.

Installing has a shape, and the shape has no gap in it for a check. Clone, install, watch the output, move on. The check belongs before the install, and before the install there is nothing to look at yet, no error, no warning, no reason to pause. A protection that fails silently creates no moment that asks to be checked. You feel safe, and feeling safe is the opposite of a prompt.

There is a second reason, quieter. npm config list sounds like a command for debugging npm itself, not for checking a repo you just cloned. It reads like something you run when installs are broken, not something you run when installs look fine. And installs that look fine are exactly the ones carrying an override, because an override does not break the install. It just changes what the install is allowed to do.

I am not going to pretend I will now run this before every install. I will not. What I will do is narrower and, I think, more honest: for a repo I do not know well, I run it inside the folder before the install, and I read the two lines that matter, the user value and the project value. A fifth of a second, and I know which file won. For a repo I know and trust, I skip it, and I skip it knowing I skipped it, which is a different thing from never having thought about it.

Problem 5: the honest limit of the check

Two limits, because the test was small. First, the check is a snapshot. It shows the config at the moment you run it. It says nothing about a repo whose config changes between the check and the install, and it says nothing about code that runs on first load, which no install setting touches at all. The check answers one question, whether the repo disagrees with your user config right now, and it answers it well. It is not a verdict on the repo.

Second, the check only helps if you read it. The output is short, but the two lines that matter sit among lines about node versions and folder paths, and a tired eye can slide past them. The tool did its part. It printed the file path and the word "overridden". The rest is on the person reading.

So the claim stands, with one correction. cryptostrapon's question pointed at a four-second check. It is not four seconds. It is under a fifth of a second, it names the file that beat your setting, and it predicts the install. The reason it never gets run is not cost. It is that the install gives you no moment to run it in, and the command sounds like it belongs to a different problem. Fix the moment, not the tool: run it inside the folder, before the install, when the repo is one you have not vetted yet.

Have you ever run npm config list before an install and caught something? Or caught a project file undoing one of your own settings in some other tool, and only found out later? I would like to hear what it was, and whether you check first now or still trust the setting and move on.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: How I Built Haze: Live WebGL Backgrounds While Learning Shaders
articles.description: So, it's been a while. Almost two years since my last article here, and work has kept me really busy....
articles.body_html:
So, it's been a while. Almost two years since my last article here, and work has kept me really busy. But I'm back, and I've got something to show you :)

Have you ever landed on a website where the background moves? Soft gradients drifting into each other, ribbons of colour, little points of light following your cursor? I've always loved those. And for a long time, I had an idea sitting in my notes app: what if adding one to your site was as easy as adding an image?

Two weeks ago, I finally shipped it. It's called Haze, and it gives you live backgrounds for your website. You pick a design, make it yours in the browser, then paste one tag into your site. It's under 9 KB, with no dependencies.

In this article, I'll walk you through why I built it, why I finally did it now, what I learned about shaders along the way, and what building it with AI was actually like. Let's jump right into it!

Just want to add one to your site? Skip to How to Use It

Where the Idea Came From

I've always been drawn to dynamic landing pages. Microinteractions, things that react when you move your mouse, and generally anything that makes a website feel alive and look different from the rest. If you've read my article on using mousemove to reveal background images, you already know this ;)

The problem is that the really nice ones are usually hard to add. You either pull in a 3D library, drop in a heavy background video, or spend hours writing shader code. That's a lot of work for a hero section.

What I wanted was something plug and play. Something I could drop into my own website or a client's project in a minute, without thinking about WebGL at all.

Why Now?

Honestly, Haze wasn't the only idea in that notes app. I've been collecting them for years, and most are small, design-related things I never found the time to build.

Two things changed this year.

First, I started the shaders section of Bruno Simon's Three.js Journey course. For the first time, the moving backgrounds I loved stopped feeling like magic, and I could see how they're actually made.

Second, AI tools got good enough that I could build an idea in days instead of months. So I figured, why not now? I picked the idea I'd held onto the longest and started there.

So, What is a Shader?

Shaders could sound intimidating, but the idea behind them is simple. Here's how I like to think about it.

Think of your screen as a grid of tiny squares called pixels. A shader is one rule that every pixel follows, all at the same time, to pick its own colour:

Your GPU (your computer's graphics chip) gets millions of pixels to follow that rule at once, about 60 times a second. That's really it!

Haze's backgrounds are just cleverer rules: ones that bend, ripple and blend colours, so you get ribbons, particles and soft gradients instead of a flat fade.

Because the GPU does all the work, the background stays sharp on any screen size, and it weighs a few kilobytes where a background video weighs megabytes. Haze also makes sure it doesn't waste your visitors' battery:

  • It stops drawing when it's scrolled off screen or the tab is hidden.
  • It shows a still frame for people who prefer reduced motion.
  • If a browser doesn't support WebGL, a CSS gradient in the same colours shows instead, so nothing breaks.

How to Use It

Here's the fun part. Go to haze.mitolu.dev, pick one of the 20 designs (ribbons, particles, paper hills, soft gradients and more), and open it in the studio. There, you can change the colours, speed and scale, and pick a cursor effect: stir, trail or pixels.

When you're happy with it, click Export and copy the tag. To use it as the background of a hero section, add the following to your HTML:

<script src="https://haze.mitolu.dev/v1/haze.js" defer></script>

<section class="hero">
  <haze-gradient preset="silk"></haze-gradient>
  <h1>Your headline</h1>
</section>

Then, in your CSS, place the background behind your content:

.hero {
  position: relative;
  isolation: isolate;
  min-height: 100vh;
}

.hero haze-gradient {
  position: absolute;
  inset: 0;
  z-index: -1;
}

And that's it! The script loads once, and <haze-gradient> draws the design wherever you put it. The tag you copy from the studio carries your own colours and settings in place of preset="silk".

If you're working in React or Next.js, you can export it as a React component instead. There's also a vanilla JS option if you'd rather not use a custom element.

Using Haze on WordPress

The easiest way is a Custom HTML block, which lets you paste the whole hero, script included.

  1. Open the page in the block editor.
  2. Click the + button, search for Custom HTML, and add the block where you want the hero.
  3. Paste the following code, and swap the line for the tag you copied from the studio: 
<script src="https://haze.mitolu.dev/v1/haze.js" defer></script>

<section style="position: relative; isolation: isolate; min-height: 80vh; display: grid; place-content: center; text-align: center; color: #fff;">
  <haze-gradient preset="silk" style="position: absolute; inset: 0; z-index: -1;"></haze-gradient>
  <h1>Your headline</h1>
  <p>A short line about what you do.</p>
</section>
  1. Click Preview to see it moving, then publish.

The styles are inline here so you don't have to touch your theme's CSS. If you're on WordPress.com, note that adding scripts needs a plan that allows plugins. Self-hosted WordPress works out of the box.

Using Haze on Framer

In Framer, you'll use an Embed component and place it behind your hero's content.

  1. Select your hero section, and set its position so its children can be pinned (Framer frames do this by default).
  2. Open the Insert menu, find Embed, and drop it inside the hero.
  3. In the Embed's settings, set the type to HTML and paste: 
<script src="https://haze.mitolu.dev/v1/haze.js" defer></script>
<haze-gradient preset="silk"></haze-gradient>
  1. Set the Embed's position to Absolute, pin it to all four edges, and set both width and height to fill the section.
  2. Move the Embed to the bottom of the layers list, so your text sits on top of it.

The <haze-gradient> element fills whatever box it's in, so once the Embed covers the section, the background does too. Preview the site to see it moving, since Framer's canvas doesn't always run embedded scripts while editing.

Two Weeks Later

I posted it on Twitter and LinkedIn, and about 120 people have tried it so far (from site analytics). That's a great start, and I'm grateful for every one of them.

But my favourite part happened in my DMs. Four people reached out because they wanted a background like this on their personal websites. Two of them said seeing my post made them want to pick up building their portfolio again, which honestly made my week.

So I helped themset it up, and each one was on a different platform:

  • a plain HTML website
  • WordPress
  • Framer
  • a Next.js app

It worked on all of them, which was exactly the point. One tag, wherever your site lives. On top of those 120 users, four real people using it on their real websites tells me the idea works.

Conclusion

And there you have it! An idea from my notes app, finally out in the world.

This is just the first version. I'm still exploring more shaders, and Haze is where everything I explore with will go next: WebGPU, textures and more designs. I've also got some more exciting updates coming soon, so stay tuned! And if you've had an idea sitting in your notes app for a while, maybe this is your sign to start!

Haze is live on Product Hunt today! If you'd like to support it, I'd really appreciate an upvote or a comment there. Support Haze on Product Hunt

Try it out at haze.mitolu.dev, and if you put one on your site, please share it with me. I'd love to see it.

If you have a question, kindly leave your feedback in the comments section.

Thanks for reading, and happy coding!

Resources for Further Learning

If this got you curious about shaders, these are the resources that helped me most:

  • An Introduction to Shaders on Frontend Horse
  • The Book of Shaders
  • Three.js Journey by Bruno Simon
  • Shadertoy: thousands of shaders you can run and tweak in the browser. Great for inspiration.
  • Yuri Artiukh's YouTube channel

articles.title: I built a 27 KB library that shows Excel files in the browser without freezing the page and named it EatSheet!
articles.description: EatSheet renders XLSX, CSV and TSV as styled HTML from a Web Worker. Here's how it works, and what matching Excel taught me.
articles.body_html:
A user uploads an .xlsx and you want to show it. Not convert it, not edit it: just show it, the way Excel would.

The usual answer is SheetJS. It reads data very well, but its free edition renders plain, unstyled HTML, the full build is 328 KB gzipped, and on a 50,000-row workbook it blocks the main thread for about a second. Your users see a frozen tab and then a grey table that looks nothing like the file they uploaded.

I wanted a viewer, not a converter. So I built EatSheet.

What EatSheet is

EatSheet is a 27 KB (gzipped), zero-dependency library that opens XLSX, CSV and TSV files and renders them as styled HTML tables. Parsing runs in a Web Worker, so the page never freezes, and on a 50,000-row workbook the first rows show up in about 140 ms.

It keeps what makes a spreadsheet readable:

  • fonts, fills, borders, alignment and wrapping
  • merged cells, hidden rows and columns, widths and heights
  • Excel number formats: currency, dates, percentages, fractions, conditional sections like [>100]
  • conditional formatting: comparisons, text rules, duplicates, top/bottom, colour scales
  • common formulas, recalculated on open (SUM, IF, ROUND and about 20 more)

It is read-only on purpose. It does not write files or open .xls, .xlsb or .ods.

50,000-row workbook EatSheet SheetJS 0.20.3
Open in Node 128 ms 546 ms
Memory 16 MB 85 MB
First view in the browser 131 ms 1,142 ms
Longest page freeze none 1,141 ms
Bundle (gzipped) 27 KB 328 KB

Medians of 7 runs on a plain-text workbook. Times vary by machine, so compare the ratios. The method is on the benchmarks page.

A complete viewer in 8 lines 

npm install eatsheet

import { openWorkbook } from 'eatsheet/worker';
import 'eatsheet/eatsheet.css';

const container = document.querySelector('#sheet'); // fixed height, overflow: auto
const book = await openWorkbook(fileOrUrl);          // File, Blob, URL, Response or ArrayBuffer

const draw = async () => (container.innerHTML = (await book.render(0, { offset: container.scrollTop })).html);
container.addEventListener('scroll', () => requestAnimationFrame(draw));
await draw();

That's the whole thing. render() returns only the rows in view, plus spacer rows that keep the scrollbar honest. Pass another index to switch sheets, and call book.close() when you're done.

If you want the data rather than HTML, read the workbook directly:

import { read } from 'eatsheet';

const book = await read(file);
const sheet = book.sheet('Summary') ?? book.sheets[0];
sheet.cell('B2'); // { type, value, style, formula?, cached?, status? }

It works with Vite and webpack 5 without configuration, in Chrome 103+, Firefox 113+ and Safari 16.4+, and in Node.js 20.12+. There are guides for React, Vue, Svelte, Angular, Next.js and Electron.

Under the hood

Everything heavy happens in a Web Worker. The main thread only sends the file in and puts HTML on the page.

  • No dependencies, including for zip. An .xlsx is a zip of XML files. EatSheet reads the zip itself and inflates each part with the browser's native DecompressionStream('deflate-raw'), so there's no bundled inflate code.
  • Cells live in typed arrays. Row, column, type, value and style each sit in a flat Uint32Array or Float64Array. Only formula cells get an object. That's why a 50,000-row workbook takes 16 MB instead of 85 MB.
  • Sheets are lazy. Shared parts (styles, strings) are read up front, and each worksheet is parsed and calculated the first time you touch it.
  • Only the window is rendered. render() builds HTML for the rows in view, and two spacer rows fill the rest of the height so the scrollbar is the right size. Scrolling just asks the worker for a new window.

What Excel taught me

The hard part wasn't parsing. It was matching Excel. I saved formula and number-format results from real Excel (16 for Mac) into a test workbook and compared EatSheet against them. That check found plenty I'd got wrong.

Excel cheats near zero, but only sometimes. In JavaScript, 0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3 is 5.55e-17. In Excel, =0.1+0.2-0.3 is exactly 0: when the final addition or subtraction differs from zero only by binary rounding, Excel snaps it. But =(0.1+0.2-0.3)+0 is not zero, because the last operation no longer cancels anything.

Excel thinks in 15 digits. Numbers are rounded to 15 significant digits before display and before functions like ROUND and INT see them. The General format shows at most 11 characters and switches to scientific notation for very large or small values.

Some answers depend on where you are. Turning text like a date or a currency amount into a number depends on the machine's locale. EatSheet can't know that, so instead of guessing it shows the result Excel saved in the file and marks the cell as such. Same for any formula it doesn't support: you get the saved value, never a wrong one.

Real files are messier than the spec. Running EatSheet against about 1,500 public workbooks from the test suites of Apache POI, LibreOffice, ClosedXML, EPPlus, ExcelJS and calamine turned up ZIP64 archives, backslashes and odd casing in part names, shared-string cells with no value, sheets without relationship ids and unescaped sheet names. Each now has its own fixture.

Uploads are hostile until proven otherwise. A spreadsheet is a zip of XML, which means zip bombs and XML entity tricks. EatSheet caps unzipped size, refuses XML entities, limits sheets, styles, merges and rendered text, and escapes every cell. Links only work for http, https and mailto, so a javascript: link stays plain text.

Try it, then try to break it

Next on the roadmap: image and chart previews, wider number-format and conditional-formatting coverage, a ready-made viewer component and print layout. Writing XLSX comes later.

  • Drop your own file into the live demo. It's parsed in your browser and nothing is uploaded.
  • Install it: npm install eatsheet (Apache-2.0, TypeScript types included).
  • Coming from SheetJS? There's a migration guide.

I'd really like to see it fail on your worst workbook. I'm paying $10 per qualifying bug (security issues, crashes or wrong data) until a $100 pool runs out. The rules are on the bounty page.

If you've fought with showing spreadsheets in a web app, I'd love to hear what broke for you in the comments.

articles.title: I indexed 2,606 legally free resources to learn the Indian stock market — here's how the no-build site works
articles.description: If you want to learn about the Indian stock market, the best material is already free. Zerodha...
articles.body_html:
If you want to learn about the Indian stock market, the best material is already free. Zerodha Varsity. SEBI and RBI investor education. NSE and BSE material. NISM study modules. OpenStax and CORE Econ textbooks. Yale, MIT and IIT-NPTEL lectures. Aswath Damodaran's whole teaching archive.

The problem is that nobody has put it in one place. So people end up with a pirated PDF that disappears in a week, a ₹15,000 course they were never going to buy, or forty open tabs with no order to them.

I built the index instead.

Live: https://85599.github.io/MarketMitra-Learn/ ·
Code: https://github.com/85599/MarketMitra-Learn

What is in it

  • 2,606 entries — 566 books, 721 PDFs, 518 videos, 473 notes, 170 papers, 129 courses, 29 tools, from 41 publishers
  • 10 calculators — SIP, SWP, goal funding, EMI, capital-gains tax, position size, futures margin, drawdown, compounding, all-in intraday trade cost
  • 80 quiz questions across 10 tracks, plus a mixed challenge
  • 87 glossary terms, each with a worked example using real Indian numbers
  • 4 learning paths that tell you what to open next
  • English and हिंदी — the entire site, not just the titles

The rule I did not break

Every link goes to the publisher's own free copy. No mirrors, no leaked PDFs, no "free download" funnels. That rules out a lot of the most-shared finance material in India, and it is the point: a link to zerodha.com/varsity does not die from a takedown.

A few build notes

No build step. The catalogue is plain JavaScript that hangs one global (window.MM). Add an object to an array, reload. The site runs from file:// and from GitHub Pages with the same files. Most contributors here will be readers, not frontend engineers, so this mattered more than tooling.

Bilingual as a data shape. Every string is either a plain string or an { en, hi } pair, and one function resolves it:

const pick = (obj) => (obj == null ? '' : typeof obj === 'string' ? obj : obj[state.lang] || obj.en || '');

No i18n library. The toggle is one variable, a re-render, and a localStorage write.

Deterministic quiz shuffling. Options must not be position-learnable, but they also must not jump around while the component re-renders. So the shuffle is seeded by the question id — FNV-1a hash, then Fisher–Yates driven by an LCG. Stable per question, different per run.

Link checking is not status === 200. Two things broke the naive checker. Some regulators answer 200 OK for bogus paths, so a dead deep link looks alive unless you assert on content. And several good publishers return 403 or 429 to curl while serving humans fine, so a status-only pass deletes real sources and keeps fake ones.

No test framework. A small Node script drives headless Chrome over CDP, clears localStorage, walks every section and asserts on what the DOM actually reports — calculator outputs to the rupee, quiz counts, chip labels. It caught a real bug: the SWP calculator divided by months instead of years, so a ₹3,338 monthly payout printed as ₹0 while every other number looked fine.

What it is not

Not investment advice. It hosts no copyrighted content. And it does not pretend that a list of 2,606 links is a curriculum — the paths, calculators and quizzes exist because the list alone is unusable.

Help wanted

Catalogue coverage (GIFT City / IFSC material, more Hindi state-board content), keeping tax and settlement constants current with each Budget, and glossary terms that still need a worked example.

MIT licensed, no CLA. Open an issue or a PR.

Written by KHUSHAL JAIN (@85599). If it saved you forty tabs, a star on the repo is the cheapest way to say so.

articles.title: TypeScript is a security liability for AI agents
articles.description: You ask your agent for a data parser. It provides the logic. It also adds a background process that...
articles.body_html:
You ask your agent for a data parser. It provides the logic. It also adds a background process that exfiltrates your environment variables. You do not see it in the diff. You run it. Your keys are gone.

Most languages give code total control over your machine. They assume a human developer is watching. AI agents do not have a conscience and they do not care about your security. They are just trying to satisfy a prompt.

I built Vow so your agent cannot reach for things you did not explicitly permit. Every function in Vow must declare its capabilities. If it needs the network, files, or environment, it uses net, uses fs, or uses env.

When you run your program with vow --sandbox, the runtime inspects those declarations before a single line executes. If the code tries to touch something off-limits, the runtime refuses to run it.

$ vow --sandbox --allow fs=./data app.vow
x SandboxError: needs capabilities
  the sandbox does not grant
  env: fn leak declares 'uses env'
Nothing was run.

The runtime stops the program cold. On November 12, 2026, I ran a test with seven attack programs. Vow blocked seven out of seven. It even has a read-only file grant. You can allow fs-read=dir to let a program read files in a directory while ensuring it is physically impossible for the code to write anything.

Vow is a programming language built for agents to write. It runs on the same loop agents use: write, run, read the error, fix.

When an agent hits a bug, it does not have to guess. Every Vow error says what is wrong, where, and the likely fix. These are repair instructions.

x TypeError: can't add a num and a str
-> line 6, col 10
6 | return "Total: " + sum
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
Likely fix: convert the number to text
first: str(sum)

Vow has no nulls and no exceptions. If a function can fail, it returns a Result value. The agent must handle it with match or the ? operator. If it fails to do that, the code will not build.

I am a high school student and I built this because I saw agents struggling with the ambiguity of modern languages. Vow is open source under the MIT license and the source is public at github.com/JakeBurwick/vow. The entire language is about 6,400 lines of JavaScript.

You can install it globally with npm.

npm install -g github:JakeBurwick/vow

If you use Claude Code, you can add an MCP server to give your agent native tools to guide, check, and run your code.

claude mcp add vow -- vow-mcp

You can find the documentation, a playground, and an llms.txt file to help your agents at https://vow-lang.vercel.app

The agent is going to keep writing code. You might as well make sure it cannot reach your environment variables while it does.

articles.title: What AI coding agents install, and what they skip
articles.description: I gave Claude, GPT, Gemini and 8 open models the same 100 build tasks. Sentry and Playwright win every time. Datadog: named 28 times, installed 0.
articles.body_html:
I build something almost every day, and these days an AI agent writes most of the code. Again and again I watched it choose the tools for me: the login library, the database, the email API. I never named one. It typed npm install, and that was the decision.

I kept asking myself three things. Why this one? Would another model pick something else? And is there a better tool out there that I never see, because I'm stuck with the model's choice?

So I started measuring it. Here's what came out of 2,188 answers from 11 models.

How I measured it

  • 100 build tasks in 20 categories: auth, hosted Postgres, ORM, payments, email, hosting, file storage, job queues, cron, feature flags, error monitoring, analytics, logging, search, vector databases, LLM tracing, CMS, realtime, end-to-end tests and UI components. They read like real requests and never name a product. One of them: "I need a hosted Postgres database for my Next.js side project. Pick one, set it up and connect to it."
  • One short system prompt for every model: you're a coding agent in the user's project, make the technical choices yourself.
  • Each task twice per model, temperature 1.0, through the public APIs.
  • Run 1 (2 Nov): Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-5.6 Terra and Gemini 3.1 Pro. 600 answers.
  • Run 2 (16 Nov): 8 open-weight models: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Qwen3 Coder Next, GLM 5.3, Kimi K2, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, gpt-oss-120b, Devstral 2 and Gemma 4 31B. 1,588 answers.
  • The pick is what gets installed: the install command first, then package.json, then the imports. A product the answer only talks about doesn't count. 60 random answers per run were checked one by one against the pick.
  • Both runs cost under $10 in API calls.

Some categories are already decided

Sentry for error monitoring and Playwright for end-to-end tests went into all 30 answers from Claude, GPT and Gemini. The open models mostly agree: Sentry in 76 of 80 answers, Playwright in 66 of 80.

In 9 of the 20 categories, one product won more than half of the big three's answers: Stripe for payments (24 of 30), Neon for Postgres (20), Drizzle over Prisma (16 to 5), Resend for email (16).

The bottom of the list matters too. Auth, feature flags and realtime have no clear winner, so there the pick still depends on the model and on how you ask.

Named isn't installed

The number I find most useful is the gap between being mentioned and being installed.

  • Supabase came up in 4 of the 30 hosted Postgres answers and was installed in none. Neon got 20. Claude, right after installing Neon's driver: "If you'd rather have auth and storage bundled too, Supabase is the alternative."
  • Datadog was named in 9 logging answers and installed in 0. The agents set up Grafana and Prometheus (12) or OpenTelemetry (10).
  • Cloudflare R2 was named 6 times, usually as "the same code with a different endpoint". The install was AWS S3 every time.
  • Mailgun was named 4 times and never installed. Resend got 16.

The open models make it even clearer. Across all 11 models, Datadog was named in 28 answers and installed in none. Mailgun: named 27 times, installed 0. R2: 14 and 0. (Supabase does better there: the open models installed it 6 times out of 80.)

A mention shows the agent knows the market. The install is the decision.

The models don't agree

Auth is the clearest case. Claude reached for Auth.js. Gemini went to Clerk. GPT wrote its own login, with sessions and password hashing, in 4 of its 10 answers.

It goes beyond auth. Claude never installed Prisma; Gemini did 4 times out of 10. GPT kept vectors in Postgres with pgvector 6 times out of 10; Gemini never did. So "what AI recommends" depends on which AI.

The open models: same defaults, three real differences

Then I ran the same 100 tasks on 8 open-weight models. I expected a different world. It mostly isn't: they install the same first pick as Claude, GPT and Gemini in 17 of the 20 categories.

The three where they don't:

  • Feature flags: Unleash first (31%). The big three go to PostHog (33%), which the open models pick only 16% of the time.
  • Logging: OpenTelemetry first (51%), not Grafana and Prometheus.
  • LLM tracing: LangSmith first (33%), Langfuse 22%. And in 38% of these answers they built the tracing themselves.

Two more patterns:

  • They build it by hand more often: 14% of all answers, against 9%. In feature flags, 28% of their answers rolled their own. In file storage, 41% installed no storage service at all; most just took the upload with Multer.
  • Single models have strong habits. Devstral 2 picked Cypress for end-to-end tests in 7 of 10 answers, where the big three never did. gpt-oss-120b sent email over plain SMTP with Nodemailer in 8 of 10. Gemma 4 picked LangSmith in 7 of 10. Qwen3 Coder and Kimi K2 went to OpenTelemetry in 8 of 10.

What I take from it

As a builder, I've stopped taking the default for granted. The model's first pick is often good. It isn't always the best tool for my case, so when it matters, I name the tool myself. And if you switch models, expect a slightly different stack from each.

If you make a dev tool, part of your funnel now runs through an agent that types the install command for the user. That reader doesn't see your landing page. It sees your package name, your docs and how short your setup is. Neon's driver goes in with one line, and the models describe Supabase as a bigger platform. That's true, and it's why Supabase ends up as the alternative and not the default.

The limits

  • These are API answers, not agents working inside a real repo with its own files and history. What's already installed would change things.
  • About 30 answers per category for the big three and 80 for the open models. Treat a gap of a few points as a tie.
  • Models change every few months, so every number carries its run date.

The data

Every prompt and every raw answer is public, free to reuse under CC BY 4.0:

  • One short write-up per finding
  • Open models vs Claude, GPT and Gemini, category by category
  • The method and the raw data

If a number looks wrong to you, say so in the comments. I'd rather fix the data than defend it.

And I'm curious: what did your agent install for you lately that you didn't expect?

I wrote this with help from my AI assistant, which also runs the benchmark. Every number comes from the published data linked above.
